    #111974. Why The US Military Is Expanding A Remote Pacific Airport To Reduce Its Reliance On Guam

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1516 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Simpleflying ↗ Open Full Page

    Why The US Military Is Expanding A Remote Pacific Airport To Reduce Its Reliance On Guam

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1516 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Simpleflying

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that in October and November, I visited the Micronesian island countries of Palau and the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM).
    • When I visited, work on the airport had not yet started, and the US military footprint on the island was minimal.
    • It has been revealed that the knowledge that Yap Island's airport was soon to be transformed was surreal.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that in October and November, I visited the Micronesian island countries of Palau and the Federated States of Micronesia (FSM). The FSM consists of four states: Yap, Chuuk, Pohnpei, and Kosrae. I visited Yap, whose airport is set to receive some major work by the United States to prepare it for war as part of the USAF's broader Agile Combat Employment (ACE) doctrine to disperse aircraft from Guam. Separately, US Navy personnel on the island informed me that there are prepares to dredge the island's harbor to allow large warships to berth. Funding has not yet been approved.

    When I visited, work on the airport had not yet started, and the US military footprint on the island was minimal. The hotel I stayed at houses around half the personnel (mostly US Navy) on the island for periods of six months. I arrived in Yap from Palau, where the minor airfield of Peleliu was closed because major construction work to expand the airport for ACE operations was underway. Here is what to know about the US's aims to expand Yap International Airport to relieve wartime strain on Andersen Air Force Base in Guam.

    It has been revealed that the knowledge that Yap Island's airport was soon to be transformed was surreal. The island is one of the remote islands in the Pacific and is difficult and expensive to reach. Adjacent to the international airport is an old Japanesee WWII airfield littered with aircraft destroyed by American bombing and lost to the jungle. I found around eight Japanese airplanes, some marked, some not marked. Here and there around the islands are the remains of lost US Vought F4U Corsairs and bombers.

    In a recent development, today, the island feels like a world away, but the USAF prepares to improve the airports and airfields on the Second Island Chain as competition with China heats up. The echoes from WWII are clear. In 1944, the US island-hopped to Japan to project airpower over the Japanese home islands.

    Recent findings suggest that now those same islands are needed to project airpower over the First Island Chain. The First Island Chain includes Taiwan, Japan's southern islands, and the Philippines. Following WWII, the US consolidated its airpower and military bases on Guam, while maintaining forward bases in Japan and Korea. The rise of China puts not only those forward bases at risk, but also Guam, which is now a prime target. Without Guam, or an effective alternative, the US's ability to project airpower over the region would diminish drastically.

    It has been revealed that the WWII US invasion of the island of Peleliu was one of the deadliest operations for the US Marines during the Pacific War. Fortunately for the native Yapese, the island was not invaded. Instead, it was intensively bombed, bypassed, and rendered irrelevant. Japanese forces remained on the island until the surrender. Most of their aircraft were destroyed in air campaigns.

    Industry observers note that the Japanese airfield is now abandoned and overgrown, but next to it, Yap International Airport operates. Yap Airport is a simple single-runway airport with a basic terminal building. The only scheduled passenger flights that use the airport are United Airlines and Pacific Missionary Aviation (PMA) United operates 737 MAX 8 flights from Guam twice weekly; this is the primary connection to the outside world. Outside of United's flights, Yap's terminal building is generally closed.

    According to recent reports, PMA operates passenger flights once a week (soon to be twice) from neighboring Palau using its two Super King Airs (seven to nine seats, depending on freight). PMA also operates flights to Yap's outlying islands as well as MEDEVAC and emergency services. I flew the PMA passenger flight from Palau to Yap, was invited on a flight to an outlying island (Ulithi), and flew out on United. PMA operates from its own private hangar and operates domestic flights from there. International (Palau) flights run through the main terminal.

    Funding for Yap Airport's transformation appears in two main categories: civilian FAA Airport Improvement Program (AIP) grants and the Department of Defense/Air Force military construction and related funding. The Air Force's Fiscal Year 2025 Military Construction budget request included around $400 million for runway extension and related work. This is labeled "PDI: Runway Extension, Inc." in the documents. The first increment funding is $96 million.

    A modest reduction appears in Fiscal 2027 documents with the explanatory note, "Program execution encountered delays and slipped from FY2025 to FY2026, funding reflects the one-time decrease after increase to support acquisition of land for an agreed upon defense site under appropriate international agreement required to complete the runway extension, parking apron, and taxiway construction at Yap International Airport, Wake Island.".

    The decrease is $31 million, but as the note includes Wake Island, it is unclear how much of this is relevant to Yap. The justification language for the funding emphasizes the need for a longer runway and facilities to support larger military aircraft for training, operations, contingency, and Agile Combat Employment. In the event of a high-end conflict with China, this likely means that Yap will be on China's list of strategic targets to be hit and neutralized.

    Industry observers note that the United States is currently upgrading numerous airports and airfields across the Second Island Chain as part of its ACE doctrine and preparations to counter China. As stated, one of the most significant programs currently underway is rehabilitating Palau's Peleliu airfield, while Angaur Airfield is already complete. On Guam, the USAF is expanding parking areas on its primary Andersen Air Force Base and rehabilitating its adjacent, formerly abandoned Northwest Field.

    One of the biggest areas of effort is on the island of Tinian in the Northern Mariana Islands. There, the USAF is expanding and rehabilitating Tinian International Airport and the formerly abandoned North Field. Nearby, the island of Rota (home to fewer than 2,000 inhabitants) has also been an area of interest and increased military exercises. The civil airports on Palau, Saipan, and Guam also factor into US ACE planning, even if no work is being carried out to expand them.

    Select Micronesian airports/airfields being expanded for ACE (per budget documents).

    One important effort is Australia. Australia is not part of the Second Island Chain, and the relationship with Washington is very different from that of small Pacific islands. In Australia, effort is mostly focused on Australia's northern RAAF bases: Tindal, RAAF Darwin, and possibly RAAF Amberley. These are being prepped primarily for US strategic bomber use with associated aerial tankers.

    Following WWII, the United States occupied the Japanese South Seas Mandate and formally took over administration as the Trust Territory of the Pacific Islands (TTPI). Eventually, the Trust Territory was broken up. The Northern Mariana Islands joined the United States as a commonwealth, while Palau, the FSM, and the Marshall Islands became independent nations with full United Nations membership.

    According to recent reports, however, sovereignty for these islands is nuanced. As part of the process, the newly independent states signed the Compacts of Free Association with the United States. Of interest to this article is that the United States retained responsibility for the defense of the islands. In practical terms, this gives the US military the benefits of basing in US territories without the islands actually being US territories.

    Sources indicate that the FSM government states, "Under the Compact, the United States provides financial assistance, defends the FSM’s territorial integrity, and allows FSM citizens unrestricted travel to the U.S. In return, the FSM grants the United States exclusive access to its land and waterways for strategic purposes." The Compact grants the United States "full authority and responsibility for security and defense matters," although in practice, the US extensively collaborates with the government rather than dictates.

    It has been revealed that visiting Yap today, it is surreal to feel so isolated and yet also see the island reprising its role as potentially returning to the frontline of a major Pacific competition. In the years ahead, the airport may start to see the deployment of US tankers and F-35 fighter jets just hundreds of feet (meters) away from the rusting hulks of Japanese Zeros and American Corsairs rotting in the jungle.

    Sources indicate that in WWII, the US Navy drew up a plan to invade Yap, but this was scrapped in favor of bombarding it and bypassing it. China’s primary counter to ACE is the continued expansion of the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force (PLARF) and supporting systems, including large inventories of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and hypersonic missiles. These are intended to hold US airfields at risk across the First and Second Island Chains.

    The US is aware of this. Increasingly, the US Air Force, Marines, and Navy are focusing on increasing the range of next-generation fighter jets (e.g., F-47 and F/A-XX). Logistics and assault requirements increasingly focus on being runway-independent, with the US Army's incoming MV-75 tiltrotor being an example. The Marines, in particular, are investing in a range of runway-independent and sea-skimming drone options for the 'last mile' of resupply and MEDEVAC.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    On September 30, 2026, we saw an unbelievably horrifying attempted terror plot, whereby a flydubai Boeing 737 first officer attempted to hijack the plane he was second in command of, and crash it into Tel Aviv’s Ben Gurion Airport.

    He attempted to kill the captain of the flight using the axe in the cockpit, but thank goodness the captain managed to open the door after being struck, so that passengers could restrain the first officer. The details that have come out ever since have been downright chilling, including how the Omani pilot had specifically sought out a job at flydubai because the airline flew to Israel, and he wanted to crash into the airport there.

    Industry observers note that ever since that incident, flydubai has been banned from flying to Israel. For that matter, air service between Israel and the United Arab Emirates is just a tiny fraction of what it previously was. However, there’s now an update, and it looks like this service could resume very soon.

    The Times of Israel reports that Israeli Transportation Minister Miri Regev has approved the resumption of flydubai flights to Israel, pending approval from Israel’s security authorities.

    This approval comes after a delegation of Israeli security and transportation officials traveled to Dubai to meet with their counterparts, to discuss new security measures to allow airlines to resume flights between Tel Aviv and Dubai.

    Emirati officials reportedly presented the Israeli officials with new steps that have been taken to ensure security in light of the incident, but details beyond that haven’t been made public. Per a statement from the Israeli Transportation Ministry:.

    “The delegation today presented Regev with the steps the organization has taken in the wake of the incident. As a result, Regev approved the return of flydubai, subject to clearance from security authorities. The move is a significant step toward restoring air connectivity between Israel and the UAE and expanding flight options for passengers.”.

    Recent findings suggest that tel Aviv was flydubai’s single biggest destination, as the airline operated in the market with up to 10 daily flights. Previously, Israeli authorities had banned flydubai from returning to the country through at least December 15, 2026.

    Let's talk about that missing rudder of Flydubai 1073 B737 MAX 8.The aerodynamic forces involved may have been large enough to cause rudder failure through aerodynamic flutter during the extreme overspeed.The aircraft descended more than 14,000 ft in under 30 seconds.Even… pic.twitter.com/ECA34H4IXG.

    Israel is typically known for its very tight security and good intelligence, but obviously there are lapses sometimes.

    One of the odd things about the flydubai attempted terror attack is that the Israeli government reportedly had a policy whereby pilots of foreign airlines couldn’t hold citizenship with countries that don’t have diplomatic relations with Israel. Oman and Israel don’t have diplomatic relations, so based on that, the first officer shouldn’t have been able to fly on the plane.

    However, it sure seems that there wasn’t actually enforcement of this rule, given that the flydubai first officer had flown to Tel Aviv several times before. I’d imagine that Israeli forces will now much more closely screen the pilots on these flights.

    I am curious if there were some upcoming policies put in place beyond that, or if the extent of the enforcement here is that it’s about the potential nationality of pilots.

    Sources indicate that israeli authorities have met with their counterparts in the UAE, and the strategy is for flydubai to be able to resume flights to Israel in the near future. This comes nearly two months after the awful terror plot, whereby a flydubai pilot intended to kill the captain, and then fly a 737 full of passengers into the terminal at Ben Gurion Airport.

    Some latest security policies have reportedly been put into place, though the details of that aren’t being made public. I think one thing is for sure — Israeli authorities will carefully be scrutinizing manifests and keeping an eye on the pilots at the controls of these flights.

    This resumption is a big deal for flydubai, given that Tel Aviv was the carrier’s biggest market.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Airports fill up with travelers, Thanksgiving meals get prepped.

    But for flyers hoping to do some cooking before their flight, there are crucial rules to know.

    The Transportation Security Administration's 3-1-1 liquids policy is still in place.

    And, yes: It applies to some of the top items you may be thinking of bringing along on your trip, from the cranberry sauce to the jar of gravy.

    “It’s weird, but sometimes we will see turkeys at security checkpoints,” former TSA spokesperson Mark Howell once told me.

    That means extra work for TSA officers, who already have to contend with one of the busiest weeks of the year at airports.

    Last year, the Sunday after Thanksgiving set the record as the busiest day ever at U.S. airports.

    If you’re among the travelers hoping to do a little meal prep at home before flying, there are some things you need to know — whether you’ll be waiting in the standard line (arrive early, if so) or heading to the TSA PreCheck line.

    According to recent reports, read more: Is air travel ready for Thanksgiving? The meltdown is over, but worries persist.

    As always, the TSA’s 3-1-1 rule governs what can and can’t come through security.

    If what you're packing doesn't meet that criteria, it needs to go in a checked bag if you want to fly with it.

    Recent findings suggest that most travelers know they can’t bring a huge bottle of sunscreen in their carry-on luggage. However, things get a bit more confusing when we start talking Thanksgiving entrees and side dishes.

    Related: When will the TSA's 3-1-1 liquids policy end?

    Let’s start with the obvious here: You have to follow the 3-1-1 rule whether you’re bringing on a mini bottle of toothpaste or your family’s famous Thanksgiving side dish.

    That means you’re good to bring a turkey, ham, chicken or something similar. Just keep in mind that the U.S. Department of Agriculture advises that you give special attention to packing and storing perishables — no one wants to eat a dish that spoiled during your flight.

    You can keep your food cool with ice packs, but they must stay frozen through the checkpoint.

    If you're bringing a frozen turkey, that also must be frozen when you pass through security. Your best bet: Leave it in the freezer until the moment you leave for the airport.

    Industry observers note that other safe bets: You're generally clear to bring stuffing, macaroni and cheese, casseroles, pies, pastries, and fresh fruits and vegetables through the checkpoint. Just be aware they may get a second look or a second trip through the X-ray machine.

    Industry observers note that with many other classic holiday dishes, you’ll want to consider the ingredients before you try to carry them on. In some cases, it’s a pretty obvious “no-go.”.

    TSA officers have historically stated that if you can "pump it, pour it, spray it or spread it," it needs to be checked — if it's more than 3.4 ounces.

    Luckily, if you’re unsure what food can come on the plane, there are a few ways to confirm before your trip.

    In a recent development, if your item falls into the “no” category for a carry-on bag, you should still be able to pack it in your checked luggage. This is a good time to use those free checked bags and other airline credits available on that travel credit card in your wallet.

    Every time the TSA catches a prohibited item while scanning a bag, it causes a delay at the checkpoint. During what’s expected to be one of the busiest weeks of the year, those delays can add up.

    Whether you blueprint to pack a bottle of hair gel or your family’s traditional Thanksgiving casserole, consider whether the size and composition of your item make it eligible to pass through security.

    On the bright side, travelers no longer have to take off their shoes when passing through security.

    Breaking: Fascinating Air Saint-Pierre Domestic Transatlantic Flight Returns In 2027

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (987 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027.
    • In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly.
    • It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    One of the most interesting transatlantic flights will be returning yet again in 2027. Maybe this will be the year I finally get to try it, even if there’s no premium cabin angle!

    In the summer of 2018, an interesting domestic transatlantic route launched — it operated seasonally once weekly. Specifically, ASL Airlines operated a Boeing 737-700 that was marketed by Air Saint-Pierre between Paris (CDG) and Saint Pierre and Miquelon (FSP).

    What’s Saint Pierre and Miquelon? It’s a self-governing territory of France, situated in the northwestern Atlantic Ocean, near Newfoundland and Labrador. The islands cover an area of about 93 square miles, and have a population of just about 6,000 people.

    The territory’s airline, Air Saint-Pierre, only has turboprops, which the carrier flies to places like Halifax (YHZ), Montreal (YUL), and St. John’s (YYT). Obviously these planes aren’t capable of operating across the Atlantic, so the airline leases a Boeing 737 for the once weekly flight.

    Sources indicate that this was the first time ever that we saw a nonstop link between these territories and mainland France. There were some other things that made this route interesting:.

    Sources indicate that the route ended up returning in 2019, was then paused in 2020 and 2021 due to the pandemic, and then returned in 2022 through 2026. The route will now be returning yet again, for the 2027 season, so it sure seems like this is basically a permanent thing.

    The once weekly flight between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Paris will be returning in 2027, between June 21 and September 6, 2027.

    The route will once again be operated by an ASL Airlines France Boeing 737-700, and the flight will be marketed and sold by Air Saint-Pierre. The flight will operate westbound on Mondays and eastbound on Tuesdays, as follows:.

    Paris to Saint Pierre and Miquelon departing 4:00PM arriving 6:30PMSaint Pierre and Miquelon to Paris departing 10:30AM arriving 8:05PM.

    Industry observers note that the 2,664-mile flight is blocked at 6hr30min westbound and 5hr35min eastbound. As you can see, the plane sits on the ground in Saint Pierre for quite a while. This is so that the crew can get their rest and operate the flight back the next day, rather than making them stay there for over a week.

    I imagine the airline is able to get a decent deal on parking at the airport for 16 hours. 😉 It’s also interesting since this is an eastbound daytime transatlantic flight, which is fairly rare.

    If you want to book a seat on this flight, below is the pricing for travel in both directions, with fares starting at €660 one-way for standard adult fares.

    As you can see, the fare difference just comes down to the age of the traveler, as well as the level of flexibility you’d like, with fares either being non-refundable and non-changeable, non-refundable but changeable for a fee, or refundable and changeable. The plane is in an all-economy configuration, as there’s no premium cabin.

    Air Saint-Pierre will be bringing back its flight between Saint Pierre and Paris in the summer of 2027, operated by ASL Airlines. This is an absolutely fascinating route, and it’s so cool to see that it was introduced in the first place, and is sticking around.

    Industry observers note that while the link between Paris and this French territory is obvious, it’s still kind of awesome that such a small territory can support a flight like this. But I guess the downside was fairly limited, since the route was subsidized from the beginning. Personally I find this to be the most intriguing transatlantic route.

    Anyone else love this Air Saint-Pierre flight as much as I do?

AFAIK I was the only passenger who was not a native French speaker. The cabin crew, while reasonably bilingual French/English, seemed more comfortable in English. Immigration and customs procedures were those of an international non-Schengen flight. St. Pierre itself is not exactly exciting, but I enjoyed two days there.

    Noel Phillips (of YT) took this flight a couple of years ago and it looked like a very interesting way to cross the pond. St. Pierre also looked like a nice, quaint place to visit. Personally, I'd be very tempted to do it.

    Tech Report: Southwest Priority Card Review: Strong Airline Benefits For Frequent Flyers

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2738 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase.
    • According to recent reports, this is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits.
    • Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Southwest Airlines has several co-branded credit cards with Chase. Of the three personal cards, my favorite one is the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    According to recent reports, this is my in-depth Southwest Priority Card review, covering the card’s benefits. I’ll also explain how despite this being the highest annual fee personal card in the portfolio, I still think it represents the best deal. Now is also a good time to consider applying for the card if you’re a fan of Southwest’s popular Companion Pass perk.

    Link: Learn more about the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Priority Credit Card.

    Before I review the Southwest Priority Card benefits in detail, here’s a high-level look at everything you need to know about the card:.

    Here are my thoughts on the Southwest Priority Card’s main pros and cons:.

    If you’re thinking about applying for the Southwest Priority Card, you’re probably most interested in the welcome bonus it’s currently offering, along with its annual fee and general eligibility rules for getting the card. So let’s dive into those. I’ll also explain a recent change to how Southwest cards factor into qualifying for the Companion Pass, which pertains to all cards, not just the Priority.

    Industry observers note that the Southwest Priority Card is offering a limited time welcome bonus: Earn 90,000 bonus points after spending $3,000 on purchases in the first 3 months from account opening. This is higher than the standard welcome offer for the card, and its minimum spending requirement should be easy for most spenders to meet.

    Recent findings suggest that rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider Rapid Rewards points to be worth 1.2 cents each. So, to me, the points from this welcome offer are worth $1,080.

    Chase and Southwest have some pretty strict rules when it comes to who is eligible for the card. The Southwest Priority Pass is not available to anyone who right now has a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card, or anyone who has received a welcome bonus on a Southwest Rapid Rewards personal card in the past 24 months. However, you are eligible if you have a Southwest business credit card.

    Sources indicate that this is in addition to Chase’s general application rules, including the 5/24 rule, whereby you typically won’t be approved for a Chase card if you’ve opened five or more newly introduced card accounts in the past 24 months. However, that’s not enforced consistently.

    Industry observers note that when it comes to credit scores, there’s not a consistent score that you need to get approved for the card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “excellent” range. That being said, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected, as it’s one of only many factors that determines card eligibility.

    In a recent development, the Southwest Priority Card has a $229 annual fee. As a point of comparison, the other personal cards have annual fees of $99 and $149, so the annual fee on this card is a bit higher. However, as I’ll explain below, the benefits could justify the premium annual fee.

    The card also has no extra cost to add authorized consumers, so you can add those for $0 each, so that authorized user spending can help you rack up rewards.

    The Southwest Priority Card has no foreign transaction fees, so this could be a useful card for your spending abroad. This is a Visa as well, and Visas are accepted pretty widely around the globe.

    Another rule worth mentioning here involves how Southwest credit card welcome bonuses help you earn the Companion Pass, which lets you bring a companion with you on flights (both cash and award tickets) and pay just taxes and fees.

    For a long time now, the points earned as part of Southwest credit card welcome bonuses have counted towards the 135,000 qualifying points needed to earn the Companion Pass. But starting soon, credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward qualification.

    According to recent reports, you’ll need to apply for a card by December 2, 2026, for your welcome bonus to count toward the Companion Pass for a final time. So apply for the Priority Card sooner rather than later if you’re hoping to earn that perk with the help of credit card spending.

    Industry observers note that now is also your last chance to get an annual boost of 10,000 Companion Pass qualifying points as a Southwest credit card holder. Starting next year, instead of a boost of 10,000 TQPs for having a Southwest card, you’ll get 10,000 TQPs if your TQP balance is 130,000 by December 31, 2027. That would be enough to get you to Platinum status, which will include unlimited Companion Pass trips as a benefit.

    This change eliminates the easiest way to earn this valuable benefit, and it’s not the only upcoming rule: referral bonuses, anniversary points, bonus points from spending, and partner spending won’t count toward the Companion Pass either. In fact, Southwest’s rolling the Companion Pass into its highest elite tier, Platinum, and requiring either 140,000 TQPs or 100 qualifying flights to earn it.

    Beyond the Southwest Priority Card airline benefits, a major draw is the card’s points earning on every purchase you make — plus how it can help you work toward Southwest elite status through earning Tier Qualifying Points.

    The Southwest Priority Card offers the following points for credit card spending:.

    According to recent reports, personally, I’d generally only put spending on the card if you’re going for A-List status and/or Companion Pass, because there are better cards for everyday spending otherwise. But still, those are some fairly solid bonus categories.

    It has been revealed that as part of an overhaul of the Rapid Rewards program, Southwest is simplifying TQP earning on credit cards. Starting in 2027, every dollar spent on a co-branded Southwest credit card will earn you one TQP. In other words, $35K in spending would earn you Silver, $65K in spending would earn you Gold, and $140K in spending would earn you Platinum.

    This earning rate is the same across cards, so this isn’t specific to the Southwest Priority Card.

    I have a dedicated post that covers how to redeem Southwest Rapid Rewards points for maximum value, but let’s briefly look at how you can use the points you earn from the Southwest Priority Card.

    Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, meaning that the value you get from your points is tied to the cash cost of Southwest tickets. There are a few different levels, ranging from Basic tickets to Choice Extra fares, so the exact value can vary a bit.

    Industry observers note that basic award fares tend to offer the best redemption value. You’ll also usually get the best value on international Southwest routes to destinations like Costa Rica and Aruba. I’ve been able to get about 2.0 cents per point on these redemptions.

    Starting in spring 2027, Southwest will add points earning and redemption opportunities with select airline partners, which should make your Rapid Rewards points more valuable for international travel. The planned partners include Icelandair, China Airlines, and Etihad Airways — I look forward to seeing how these add value to the program.

    One great thing about the Southwest Rapid Rewards program is that there are no change or cancellation fees, and rebooking a fare when the price drops gets you a refund equal to any difference in points. Just note that Basic fares can only be changed by upgrading to a higher fare bundle, so for a cheaper Basic award you’d cancel and rebook rather than change.

    As Southwest’s highest annual fee personal credit card, the Southwest Priority Card has the most benefits, including several that can improve your travel experience with the airline. Here are the card’s most notable ongoing perks.

    Industry observers note that southwest Priority Card holders can select a Preferred seat on Southwest at the time of booking for no extra charge. If Preferred seats aren’t available on your flight, you should be able to select a standard seat for free. Preferred seats are located near the front of the cabin, so having one usually means you’ll board and deplane faster.

    Sources indicate that preferred seats generally cost about $30 to $60 extra, and selecting free Preferred seats at booking is a perk of Southwest Silver elite status. If you don’t have status and you’re able to use this benefit, you could get real value even after just a few Southwest flights.

    Industry observers note that the Southwest Priority Card also offers unlimited upgrades to extra legroom seats within 48 hours prior to departure. This perk applies to the main cardholder as well as up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation.

    Extra legroom seat prices vary by route, but they generally cost roughly $40 to $100. On a route where they’re at the higher end of this range and you have multiple companions on your reservation, you could even recoup the Priority Card’s annual fee through one trip alone.

    Keep in mind that complimentary extra legroom seats within 48 hours of departure is another benefit of Southwest Silver status. So if you have that level of status or higher already, you don’t need the Priority Card to enjoy this perk.

    The Southwest Priority Card gets the primary cardholder and up to eight additional passengers on the same reservation a first checked bag at no additional cost. Checked bags on Southwest cost $45 each way, so this can save you up to $90 roundtrip on checked bag fees per person.

    With even a couple of roundtrip flights per year, this benefit can offset the annual fee — and about five one-way checked bags per year could cover it as well.

    With the Southwest Priority Card, you’ll be able to board with Group 5, or earlier if you have elite status or a fare or seat type that qualifies you for an earlier boarding group.

    Southwest has eight total boarding groups, so while there are several ahead of Group 5, it’s better than boarding last. This benefit applies to the main cardholder and up to eight passengers on the same reservation.

    On your Southwest Priority Card anniversary every year, you’ll receive 7,500 bonus Rapid Rewards points. Southwest Rapid Rewards is a revenue-based frequent flyer program, and you can generally expect that you’ll need around 83 Rapid Rewards points for every dollar of airfare you book.

    In other words, 7,500 bonus points get you around $90 in Southwest airfare annually. That covers more than a third of the annual fee right there.

    Recent findings suggest that if you pay with your Southwest Priority Card you can save 25% on inflight Wi-Fi and drink purchases. You’ll receive statement credits for the 25% within two billing cycles of your purchase (though usually much faster than that).

    The Southwest Priority Card offers a variety of travel & purchase protection benefits, including:.

    Of course, you’ll want to check the cardmember agreement for the full terms & conditions associated with these benefits.

    Even though the Southwest Priority Card has the highest annual fee of any personal Chase Southwest card, it might be worthy of consideration.

    Many people love flying Southwest for the ability to earn the Southwest Companion Pass, the lack of change fees and vouchers that don’t expire. For others, Southwest is just a practical airline to fly on occasion, given its massive route network. Regardless, there’s lots of value in having points and benefits on Southwest.

    That said, not everyone needs a Southwest credit card — and even among Southwest credit cards, there’s a cheaper option that could make more sense if you only fly the airline a few times a year. Let’s look at some alternatives and how they stack up.

    It has been revealed that first, here’s a look at how the Southwest Priority Card compares to the other two personal Southwest cards. Note that all three cards have the free checked bag benefit and Group 5 boarding, so I left that out of the comparison table here.

    The Southwest Rapid Rewards® Premier Credit Card (learn more) is one step down from the Southwest Priority Card, with a $149 annual fee and slightly pared-down perks. If you care about getting complimentary Preferred seat selection at the time of booking, the Priority Card is a better pick, since the Premier Card only offers this within 48 hours of departure.

    Other differences between the Priority and Premier cards include:.

    The Southwest Premier Card could be a decent alternative if you want a lower annual fee and don’t care about the lower earning rate on Southwest and caps on the other bonus categories.

    Recent findings suggest that there’s also the Southwest Rapid Rewards® Plus Credit Card (learn more). This is the entry-level personal Southwest credit card, with a $99 annual fee. As you’d expect, it has the fewest benefits among the personal Southwest cards. Here’s a quick breakdown:.

    I think the Southwest Priority Card provides significantly more value than the Southwest Plus Card, so the higher annual fee could still be worth it.

    It has been revealed that if you’re looking to complement your Southwest Priority Card with a Southwest business card, consider the incredible Southwest® Rapid Rewards® Performance Business Credit Card (learn more). This card has some nice perks, including:.

    Chase Ultimate Rewards is a transfer partner with Southwest Rapid Rewards, and points transfer at a 1:1 ratio. As a general rule of thumb, you’re going to earn points at a faster rate through Ultimate Rewards than through Rapid Rewards, not to mention that your points have a lot more flexibility.

    Should you earn Rapid Rewards points directly with a Southwest card, or with a Chase Ultimate Rewards card?

    For context, some of the best cards for earning Chase Ultimate Rewards points include the following:.

    On top of that, the following four no annual fee cards earn points that can be converted into Ultimate Rewards points at a 1:1 ratio in conjunction with one of the above cards:.

    When providing credit card advice, my answer to whether or not it makes sense to get a certain card is usually “it depends.” and this is the case as well with the Southwest Priority Card, especially given the latest changes to the Southwest Rapid Rewards program.

    If you fly Southwest several times a year and want a free checked bag and complimentary Preferred seat selection, not to mention complimentary extra legroom upgrades, this card can be well worth it. That’s especially true if you don’t have elite status with Southwest already, since it offers some of these same benefits.

    In a recent development, if you’re interested in the Priority Card and also want the chance to earn the Companion Pass, consider applying sooner than later. Southwest credit card welcome bonuses will no longer count toward Companion Pass qualification in 2027, and this card’s 90,000-point welcome offer can get you a good chunk of the way there.

    If you want to learn more about the Southwest Priority Card, follow this link.

    #111968. Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1166 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Onemileatatime ↗ Open Full Page

    Why I’ll Never Fly Ryanair, Even If It’s The Only Option

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1166 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world.
    • Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.
    • It has been revealed that that said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that love them or hate them, low-cost airlines dominate the skies in some parts of the world. Nowhere is that more true than in Europe, home to Ryanair, the largest low-cost airline in the world (per 2025 passenger numbers).

    Back in my late teens and early 20s, I was all for booking the cheapest ticket to a place I’d never heard of, just because I could.

    It has been revealed that that said, I still do still love to find a bargain, and can spend hours researching the best value option even when booking the simplest of itineraries. The buck stops, however, at Ryanair. My last flight was in 2023, and despite nothing glaringly awful happening, I vowed it would be the last.

    Part of the low-cost airline business model is choosing airports far from the cities they serve, since landing fees are often cheaper. One of the best examples of this is Frankfurt Hahn (HHN), located about 80 miles from Frankfurt am Main — the city the airport’s named after.

    Recent findings suggest that after a quick check on the Uber app, a one-way Uber ride would likely cost around $180. A more wallet-friendly alternative would be this €24 bus. The journey time would likely be longer than the flight itself….

    Even Ryanair’s largest base at London Stansted (STN) is around 40 miles from London, and requires a relatively expensive train or lengthy bus journey to the city.

    This is the part I hate the most about Ryanair. They are so stingy that they built their planes with built-in steps at the front boarding door so they don’t have to pay for air bridges. Whether it’s a sizzling 110+ degrees in the middle of the day in Seville, or deep in the minuses at Rovaniemi in Finland (the gateway to Lapland and Ryanair’s northernmost airport), you’ll have to brace the elements while boarding and deplaning.

    According to recent reports, getting a deal on a flight departing at daft o’clock in the morning isn’t limited to just Ryanair or low-cost airlines. Who would ever want to set an alarm before 6 a.m.? However, Ryanair can charge such a premium to fly at a respectable time of day, that its fares end up almost the same as flag carriers.

    It has been revealed that the screenshot below is a great example. British Airways’ one-way fares of 88 pounds from Heathrow (LHR) are over twice as much as two of Ryanair’s options from Stansted to Berlin.

    However, Ryanair charges £74 for its midday departure (without a cabin bag). Compare that to BA’s 1:20 p.m. departure for £88 including a cabin bag; it’s a wonder why anyone would even consider Ryanair’s option if they needed to fly in the middle of the day.

    Recent findings suggest that ultimately, airline preference is very subjective, and I know there are some die-hard Ryanair fans who won’t hear a bad word said about the airline. In its defense, if you’re heading somewhere off the beaten track, you can usually rely on Ryanair to get you as close as possible.

    Personally, I’d rather enjoy status benefits (and earn miles and status-earning points) by flying a legacy carrier like Air France-KLM, British Airways, or Lufthansa to the closest airport, then figure out ground transportation the rest of the way.

    Where do you stand on flying Ryanair?

    Newly introduced FAA Rule For Planes Lining Up On Runways May Cause Delays

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1045 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Onemileatatime

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some upcoming restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.
    • As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a newly introduced rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports.
    • To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has just added some upcoming restrictions to how air traffic controllers can clear aircraft to “line up and wait” on the runway, in anticipation of takeoff clearance. This is intended to add an extra safety buffer, but to quote an airline pilot on an ATC frequency, “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    As of today (November 24, 2026), the FAA has introduced a newly introduced rule regarding how aircraft can be cleared onto runways at airports. Air traffic controllers want to utilize runways as efficiently as possible for both takeoffs and landings, and that often involves having planes line up on the runway and wait, in anticipation of takeoff clearance.

    To give an example, sometimes a plane will be cleared for takeoff, and then a bit of separation is required until the next plane can depart. In those situations, it’s common for the air traffic controller to clear that next plane to “line up and wait.”.

    Industry observers note that the idea is that the plane then has clearance to enter the runway, and then await further takeoff clearance. After all, it might take 30 seconds or so for a plane to taxi from the hold short point of the runway, to getting into position on the runway.

    In a recent development, under the fresh FAA rules, air traffic controllers will only be allowed to clear pilots to “line up and wait” in situations where there’s a dedicated supervisor or controller-in-charge who can’t perform other duties while these operations are underway. In the past this was a recommendation, but now this is a rule.

    Industry observers note that given constant air traffic control staffing shortages, this could actually impact operations a good percentage of the time. Here’s how the reason for this policy change is described:.

    The core purpose of this change is to elevate the safety standard for Line Up and Wait (LUAW) operations by removing ambiguity in staffing requirements. By upgrading the guidance from “should” (a recommendation) to “must” (a mandatory requirement), the FAA ensures that the personnel providing watch supervision (OS/CIC) are fully dedicated to overseeing the safety of the operation without the distraction of simultaneously managing other operational tasks.

    I can appreciate the concept behind this, which is to improve safety. After all, we have air traffic controllers who are spread too thin, and all too often, they get a bit distracted due to the volume of things they have to deal with. That has definitely been a contributing factor to many accidents and incidents over the years.

    I do find the timing of this being introduced to be interesting, as it comes during one of the busiest travel periods of the year. I don’t think this will actually lead to any major complications, and for that matter, safety shouldn’t be compromised just because flights are busy.

    If you’re an observant passenger who is always looking out the window and is on Flightradar24, you may notice this policy in practice, for situations where you feel like the plane should already be lining up on the runway, but isn’t.

    I can’t imagine this policy change will lead to any major delays on a widespread basis, but then again, given how at capacity many airports are, even a little change can make a big difference. Below you can hear some talk between an air traffic controller at Albuquerque Airport (ABQ) and a Southwest pilot, where they’re discussing the change. As you can hear, the pilot says “that’s probably going to cause some delays, that’s for sure.”.

    A upcoming FAA runway safety requirement takes effect across the United States tomorrow, November 24, and an air traffic controller in Albuquerque is already warning pilots about possible delays.The change requires airports to have a dedicated supervisor on duty before controllers… pic.twitter.com/zxXariHNAy.

    Industry observers note that while the FAA is making changes intended to improve safety, how about also requiring air traffic controllers in the United States to start using standard phraseology, like everywhere else in the world? 😉.

    Industry observers note that as of today, the FAA has added a latest restriction on planes being able to line up on runways. A “line up and wait” procedure is pretty standard, but will now only be allowed in situations where the air traffic controller is only focused on one thing. Given how short staffed air traffic control often is, this could have some implications.

    I don’t think this will meaningfully slow things down on a national level, but for airports that make the most of every second to get planes in and out, it could definitely have implications.

    What do you make of the FAA’s upcoming restrictions on takeoff?

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).
    • If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday demonstrated how poisonous the politics could become.
    • Industry observers note that budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said he wants to fix Social Security, while also calling it a "Ponzi scheme." (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    If Congress ever tries to fix Social Security to address a looming shortfall, a Senate Budget Committee hearing Wednesday demonstrated how poisonous the politics could become.

    Industry observers note that budget Chairman Ron Johnson, R-Wis., set the stage for a fierce partisan clash even before the hearing began by calling Social Security a "Ponzi scheme" in a Fox Business interview earlier in the day. Democrats erupted, accusing Johnson of scaring seniors and being unwilling to fix a financial lifeline for more than 72 million retirees.

    “I think it’s outrageous,” stated Sen. Mark Warner, D-Va., one of several Democrats on the panel who slammed Johnson for his comments. “Don’t go out there scaring Americans to make political points on Fox News. This is too fricking important.”.

    Johnson acknowledged making an “imprecise comment” on prospects for a fix during the Fox interview. But he also told Democrats that if they had read his “chairman’s memo” he sent them Tuesday they would know he wants to preserve the system and pass a law to prevent any cuts to benefits if the Social Security Trust Fund is depleted.

    Sources indicate that "This is a scam, it’s grotesque, and at this point there’s really no way to fix Social Security," he said on Fox Business. "It’s a Ponzi scheme. You can’t fix it. You just shut it down and hope you can recover some of your money.”.

    But Johnson appeared to contradict himself later in the same interview, saying there is a difference with a “government-sanctioned Ponzi scheme” in that “you can force investors to keep putting money into it and that’s what we’ll probably have to do … You can fix Social Security and make it solvent.”.

    In his opening statement at the hearing, Johnson said Congress should pass a law to prevent benefit cuts and then “roll up our sleeves and begin seriously addressing the main problem, our massive debt and deficits.” He said that is the only way to “ensure we have the financial wherewithal to honor promises made to seniors.”.

    It has been revealed that johnson also told the panel he used the term “Ponzi scheme” in part to draw attention to the importance of addressing the problem. “If I gotta pay a political price for that, I really don’t care,” he said.

    There is no doubt that a fix is needed. Without any change, Social Security recipients face a 22 percent cut in benefits by the end of 2032, according to projections from the Social Security Board of Trustees. Johnson said Congress and the president won’t cut benefits even if the trust fund is exhausted.

    And there has been no shortage of Social Security bills introduced to provide a fix, but none of them has gained momentum.

    Sources indicate that sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, drew flak from fellow Republicans after he and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., proposed lifting the cap on income subject to the Social Security payroll tax so that the tax would apply to all earned income.

    Sources indicate that A bipartisan proposal, from Sens. Richard J. Durbin, D-Ill., Bill Cassidy, R-La., Tim Kaine, D-Va., and John Cornyn, R-Texas, would have put a strategy in motion by requiring the Social Security Advisory Board to recommend a bill that would ensure Social Security is funded for at least the next 50 years.

    Senators on both sides of the aisle remarked they were committed to fixing Social Security. Republicans stressed the importance of economic growth to bring in more revenue to the system and cautioned that tax increases would slow growth.

    Democrats pitched shifting more revenue into the system, for example by raising the cap on the payroll tax or taxing other income.

    “I do believe if we can be focused on fixing the Social Security stability concern, that could be a stepping stone to fixing broader problems,” said Kaine, who is anticipated to chair the Budget Committee when Democrats take over Congress next year.

    BermudAir, the unusual boutique carrier that launched operations a few years back, keeps getting stranger. The organization has just declared a massive expansion for the summer of 2027, and with this, we’ll see the airline add all kinds of seemingly random routes to and from Bermuda, plus all kinds of routes that don’t touch Bermuda.

    Whether you want to fly from Nashville to Ocho Rios, or from Fredericton to Bermuda, the airline now has you covered!

    It has been revealed that for a little bit of background, in mid-2023 we saw the launch of BermudAir, a quirky niche airline with the goal of operating Embraer jets between Bermuda (BDA) and the United States and Canada. Initially the airline was going to operate all-business class planes, but it scrapped (“delayed”) that concept before launch, instead introducing a two-cabin concept (though business class just has blocked adjacent seats and better service).

    As I said from the beginning, the whole thing struck me as an odd venture, essentially trying to serve Bermuda year-round profitably, while going up against the major carriers that serve the airport.

    To my surprise, the airline is still in business over three years after launch, though it hasn’t necessarily been that smooth. As is pretty common for an airlines startup, the first years have been rocky, with several routes being cut after launch. For that matter, the airline faced a lawsuit over millions in unpaid airport fees at its hub, which isn’t exactly a great sign.

    Several months back, BermudAir unveiled upcoming winter 2026-2027 seasonal flying to places other than Bermuda. Now the airline has announced summer seasonal flying for 2027, and it’s arguably even stranger. The routes are all over the place.

    In the summer of 2027, BermudAir will fly from Bermuda (BDA) to the following destinations:.

    On top of that, the airline will be expanding beyond Bermuda, with fresh seasonal services in the following markets:.

    Sources indicate that I really can’t make sense of what is going on at BermudAir. I feel like we’ve had reasons to be suspicious, when you look at the initial business model, vs. how things have played out:.

    Industry observers note that I’m not suggesting there’s no demand in any of these new markets. The demand may very well be there. But there are a lot of challenges here:.

    According to recent reports, what’s interesting here is how the airline announced seems to be taking a similar strategy both for this winter and for next summer. So based on the fact that the airline is moving forward with its current winter schedule, maybe this is working? I don’t know….

    Sources indicate that it’s also interesting how the airline actually got permission to operate these routes. As a reminder, Bermuda, Anguilla, and Turks & Caicos, are all British Overseas Territories, and Belize and Jamaica are former British Overseas Territory. How does the airline get permission to serve places like Honduras, though? I guess the airline is somehow getting permission to operate this as fifth freedom service, or something.

    In a recent development, bermudAir is expanding rapidly, as the airline has announced new routes for the summer of 2027. Not only does this include several new routes to Bermuda (including out of Fredericton!), but the airline is also adding flying between the United States and Grand Cayman, Honduras, Jamaica, etc.

    I think BermudAir deserves an award for the most unusual route network of any “real” airline. I certainly can’t think of any other airline in this “league.”.

    Populism, for all of its faults, can be a powerful force in politics when it is rising. While populist agendas can come in many different varieties, they are all propelled by a broad sense that the people — or more properly, The People — are being held back by some elite force, whether that be Big Business or an insular political establishment or something darker. If only we can overcome the enemy, we are told, we will sweep to victory on the broad, sunny uplands.

    It has been revealed that as I’ve noted before, the very nature of populism is that it has to redefine The People to include something less than all the people when it inevitably encounters the reality that its premises are not universally shared. And so it goes from there, because populism always sooner or later must decide to cling to its narratives when forced to choose between them and empirical reality:.

    America’s leading natural gas competitor is on track to become its biggest customer. With traffic down through the Strait of Hormuz, Qatar is betting on U.S. liquefied natural gas (LNG). The state’s energy tech giant, QatarEnergy, signed two purchase agreements for American LNG in late October and is reportedly in talks with U.S. supplier Venture Global for a third. There may yet be more deals coming down the pike, including one with Houston-based NextDecade. QatarEnergy already owns 70 percent of Golden Pass LNG, a joint venture with ExxonMobil that shipped its first cargo out of Sabine Pass, Texas, in April.

    Doha’s ventures are adding up. So much so that, according to an early November Financial Times report, Qatar may become “the biggest U.S. LNG buyer” by 2033. This presents the United States with opportunities to affirm market leadership and drive a wedge between Doha and Tehran.

    Industry observers note that natalie Ecanow is a research analyst for the Foundation for the Defense of Democracies. Her work focuses on the Middle East.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that they tell me this is their biggest sale of the year, and the biggest they expect to offer for the foreseeable future. It matches the 30% discount I covered in August.

    Readers who took advantage of the offer before their March price increase did better: $79 for the first year and $99 for renewals. That offer’s gone. The regular annual prices are now $129.99 and $189.99, and their price lock guarantee applies to those full prices, not the discounted first year.

    I’ve noted this is one of the better services for finding rare premium cabin awards. They search departures from more than 200 airports in the U.S. and Canada, and you choose which airports you want alerts for. You can stick to your home airport or include other cities you’re willing to position to.

    Deals arrive by email, there’s an online hub where you can browse them, and you can opt into text alerts for mistake fares and their rarest “unicorn” deals. They say they’ve recently sent more than 80 flight alerts in a month, including more than 30 business class award alerts, such as:.

    Most alerts won’t fit any one person’s plans. I like this most for someone with transferable points who can let award availability help decide where to go. Finding one useful business class award can easily justify the subscription. If you need a particular flight on a particular date, though, a stream of deals to other places isn’t going to solve that.

    They’ve also added FareTracker. Premium members can track up to 10 cash flights and get an email when the price drops by at least $20, with instructions to rebook and claim the difference as an airline credit. You still need a fare whose rules allow that, and you have to do the rebooking. But it’s a useful reason to keep watching a ticket after you’ve bought it.

    In a recent development, the Premium+ bundle adds hotel deals, including difficult award availability and discounted paid stays. Recent alerts have included Park Hyatt Kyoto and the renovated Waldorf Astoria Fresh York. The extra $42 makes sense if you’d build a trip around finding award nights at a property like that.

    #111955. Industry News: Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1238 w)
    📖 Baca
    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Trump banks on personal relationships moving Putin, Xi toward U.S. interests

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1238 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S.
    • That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.
    • “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, russian President Vladimir Putin, Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump arrive for a trilateral meeting in Shenzhen, China, on Thursday. (Win McNamee/AFP via Getty Images).

    That was the greeting, complete with a lengthy handshake, President Donald Trump gave Vladimir Putin before two high-level meetings Thursday, including the first “trilateral” session with sitting U.S., Russian and Chinese heads of state.

    “It’s nice to see you,” Trump told Putin before a private one-on-one meeting in China’s Shenzhen economic zone, before pulling the Russian strongman close and saying something into his ear too low for journalists’ microphones to pick up.

    Sources indicate that trump and Putin then posed for the cameras with wide grins, again underscoring the U.S. president’s closeness with a world leader who has been partially shunned by the West since he released a war with Ukraine in February 2022. Trump on Thursday also appeared several times alongside Chinese President Xi Jinping, who like Putin has been scorned by Republican and Democratic lawmakers for years.

    “We’ve had a great relationship for many years. We've known each other for a long time. And I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this — or, at least, start,” Trump told reporters as Putin beamed from a few feet away.

    They later were joined by Xi for a group photo before sitting down at a round wooden table with a large arrangement of pink flowers in the center.

    His interactions with and comments about Putin and Xi reflect Trump’s belief that his personal relationships can bend them toward U.S. interests. But that gambit clashed Thursday with his second term’s expiration date — the White House did not disclose any agreements reached during his various meetings with the two leaders, nor did Trump hold a press conference following the three-way session.

    Industry observers note that both Putin and Xi are adept at playing the geopolitical long game. The 26 months left in Trump’s term is a relatively short amount of time compared to the duo that has been in power for a combined 56 years and will remain in place for the foreseeable future.

    Indeed, even Trump acknowledged the first-ever meeting might not immediately yield much progress on its ostensible goal: paring each powers’ nuclear weapons arsenals.

    According to recent reports, “I must say, it's, quite frankly, a very hard thing to do, because once you have the nuclear weapons, it's very hard to not have them. It's very hard to give them up as the leader of a country,” Trump stated as Putin and Xi looked on. “Something that's very difficult to say, because … it's the way life works.

    Industry observers note that “You know, you have thousands of weapons and you're supposed to give them up, and yet you have countries in addition to us, in much smaller numbers, but they have nuclear weapons, also,” he added. “So it's not an easy thing to do and give them up.”.

    Trump, who was convicted by a Upcoming York jury in a business records case and who saw a federal election interference case against him dismissed only because of his reelection, also appeared to join Putin’s resistance to international criminal justice entities that have alleged Putin has committed war crimes in Ukraine.

    “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I'll be suggesting ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction,” Trump said, a statement that would be almost unthinkable to hear from any other sitting U.S. president.

    Other world leaders, including democratically elected ones, at two Pacific region economic summits in which Trump participated this week did not receive the kind of cordial and personal treatment from the U.S. side that Putin and Xi enjoyed.

    And other world leaders and congressional Democrats this week expressed concern with Trump's closeness to the Russian and Chinese strongmen.

    Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., on Thursday called the unprecedented summit a “historic embarrassment.” He criticized Trump for leaving the meeting without any apparent concrete commitments from Moscow or Beijing on a number of issues, including curbing Chinese espionage inside U.S. companies and ending the Ukraine conflict.

    “This summit was nothing but a glorified photo op and a gift to Putin and Xi,” Schumer stated.

    Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk wrote this Thursday on X, shortly after Trump’s warm greeting for the former KGB officer: “God, protect us from such friends.”.

    In a recent development, nicolas Burns, a former senior U.S. diplomatic official under GOP and Democratic presidents, was critical of Trump’s meetings with Xi. He said it was “key” for U.S. and Chinese leaders to hold talks, but added: “We need stability in the relationship with China — but there’s a but.”.

    “The president seems to be following a detente policy with China, with very little substance. There’s a lot of pomp and circumstance, red carpets, a lot of nice words,” the former ambassador to China, NATO and Greece told “Morning Joe” on MS NOW. “Too friendly with Xi Jinping, who’s not going to be swayed by rosy words from President Trump.”.

    Even before Trump met with the Russian and Chinese leaders behind closed doors, Republican and Democratic lawmakers noted they doubted very much would come from it.

    “I want nuclear weapons to be reduced. As you know, China has been unwilling to even have a conversation with the United States about nuclear arms reduction until they reach a certain plateau in the number of weapons that they have,” House Armed Services Committee Vice Chair Rob Wittman, R-Va., told reporters Tuesday.

    “I'm glad that they're willing to have the conversation. We do need a limit, as you know,” added Wittman, who lost his reelection bid earlier this month. “Right now, neither Russia nor China has a nuclear arms reduction treaty with the United States. It would be nice for us to actually have one.”.

    Industry observers note that sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., an Armed Services Committee member, wanted Trump to press Putin over Ukraine.

    It has been revealed that “Ukraine is defending itself from Putin's aggression, which this president should be opposing as well,” Blumenthal stated Tuesday. “We are spending no money on Ukraine. Let's be very clear: Arms to Ukraine are purchased by Ukraine with financial support from Europe, not America. … Let's support Ukraine.”.

    Recent findings suggest that on spending, Trump and administration officials have been pressing Senate Republicans to rapidly pass another budget reconciliation measure with $350 billion more for the Defense Department. However, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., and other GOP senators have signaled in the last 24 hours that they had shelved the notion of another fast-track spending measure.

    “You have to have a path forward. You've got to get on it, and you have to protect it, and that takes 50 in the Senate,” Thune told reporters Thursday. “And then you've got to get it through the House. As you probably saw yesterday, a lot of folks in the House were lobbing grenades at the Senate reconciliation bill and complaints about it not being offset, et cetera. So, you know, in my view at least, you want to have a path forward to success.”.

    John M. Donnelly and Jackie Wang contributed to this report.
