    #111953. Why Airport Food Costs So Much—High Rents, Costly Operations And Price Rules Shops Get To Work Around

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 35m • 📚 Deep Dive (7063 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Why Airport Food Costs So Much—High Rents, Costly Operations And Price Rules Shops Get To Work Around

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 35 min read (7063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~35 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that A $7 bottle of airport water is bad enough.
    • There’s a latest, good investigation into airport food prices with the reporter comparing terminal prices with stores outside the airport, then confronting the people supposedly enforcing the rules that prices are supposed to match.
    • Recent findings suggest that I detest the hypocrisy here, but the video largely dismisses the economics that explain those rules, the exceptions, and the weak enforcement.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that A $7 bottle of airport water is bad enough. Being told the airport protects you from excessive prices, while it approves the price and collects money from the shop, is actually worse. There’s a newly introduced, good investigation into airport food prices with the reporter comparing terminal prices with stores outside the airport, then confronting the people supposedly enforcing the rules that prices are supposed to match. Airports usually defended the prices. I detest the hypocrisy here, but the video largely dismisses the economics that explain those rules, the exceptions, and the weak enforcement. Those are the reasons we get both the pricing promises and the prices that don’t match. Airports make concessions expensive to operate, then collect money from businesses selling to passengers who have limited alternatives. The starting point is understanding that passengers aren’t the customer, they’re the product. The Airport Sells Access To You An airport sells merchants access to people who have already cleared security, can’t easily leave, and may have only 20 minutes before boarding. You can compare restaurants, and if you did the different brands are often run by the same tech giant with products sourced from the same vendor. And airport concession agreements frequently include not just rent but the greater of a minimum guaranteed payment or a percentage of sales. The airport wants successful merchants. Their sales support its budget. And airlines can benefit, too. Dallas–Fort Worth’s 2025 budget showed $120.1 million of non-airline net revenue going toward terminal costs and another $23.9 million toward airfield costs, reducing what airlines otherwise had to pay. That money came from parking but also concessions like restaurants. I’ve written about airports treating passengers as the product for years. The clearest example is removing moving walkways so people stop bypassing the shops. Dallas–Fort Worth approved a roughly $1 million project to remove walkways in terminal D and add retail and restaurant seating. The airport’s concessions executive remarked the project was expected to generate about $2 million in revenue within two years. Similarly, United removed the eight moving walkways inside Chicago O’Hare’s C concourse. Getting you to your gate efficiently and getting you to wander into shops and spend money are in tension, and there’s a strong preference for the latter. Street Pricing Depends On Which Street You Choose Many airports promise that vendors will charge the same prices as comparable businesses outside the airport, or those prices plus an allowed premium. The airport industry’s 2025 concessions survey found street pricing plus a percentage at 80% of responding large hubs. Chicago’s sample concession agreement calls for value pricing tied to approved off-airport stores, without a general percentage premium. The Port Authority Of New York New Jersey’s manual uses three to six approved comparison locations. Branded restaurants and shops generally must be compared with locations of the same brand. In the video, the Port Authority defends a $6.89 bottle of water by saying Hudson is a specialty market rather than a bodega. That’s especially rich given that its own manual describes travel essentials shops as also being known as news and gift shops or convenience stores, and specifically requires comparisons for bottled drinks and snacks. At Denver, most of the high prices out of sync with off-airport were expressly approved by the airport. Airport Starbucks are often compared to other airports rather than non-airport locations. You Can’t Wish Away The Cost Of Operating Inside An Airport I’ve explained why airport restaurants are expensive to operate. Rent is only part of it. Hiring is harder. Employees have to get to the airport, often park remotely and take a shuttle, clear security, and have to pass background checks. That limits the pool of available workers, makes the job less attractive, and drives up wages needed to attract employees. Deliveries require more handling. Supplies have to be screened and brought through controlled routes and delivery windows. Some airports require centralized distribution. DFW just opened a 90,000 square foot receiving and distribution center. Screening, facilities and handling and third parties that manage those add costs. Space and construction are expensive. There’s limited storage, kitchens face airport constraints, and building or renovating behind security is harder than fitting out a storefront in a strip mall. The airport controls the operating schedule. Merchants may have to open early and serve late flights even when those hours aren’t profitable. High prices at peak cross-subsidize slow times where merchants must remain open. The video answers the cost argument largely by pointing to high passenger volume. But merchants bid for that valuable traffic, and some of the benefit gets captured by the airport through rent and concession payments. Nor is expensive rent entirely an outside force the airport suffers from. The airport is the landlord. It’s choosing how much revenue to extract, what operating conditions to impose, and which merchants get access to the passengers. Many airports impose even higher wage costs than the market would require on its own. That costs money, too. But since U.S. airports are predominanelty owned by government, there’s political pressure to claim that passengers are being protected from the high prices that result from the government airport’s own policies. Airports Even Approve Fees To Get Around Their Own Caps Sometimes there’s no need to fudge price comparisons to support higher pricing needed to cover an airport’s higher cost environment. The airport passes a rule to allow vendors to charge more on top of the allowed price. I’ve covered airports allowing surcharges alongside their street pricing rules. The Port Authority’s current regulation permits a separate employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%, on top of its street price plus 15% rule. (And that ‘wage and benefit fee’ doesn’t actually go to workers as such.) Earlier this month I covered a JFK self-checkout purchase of a $21.99 book carrying a 3% employee retention fee. I’ve also covered Minneapolis’s earlier 4.5% hospitality surcharge, with a sign explaining that it isn’t a tip: Then there’s the tip screen. In Austin, I couldn’t pay by card at self-checkout for a bottle of water without entering at least a penny as a tip. Zero wasn’t an option, and entering a tip manually rejected $0. A separate Austin self-checkout I flagged in January defaulted to 18% while adding a card processing surcharge. Portland Highlights The Rules Can Work When The Whole Deal Works None of this means street pricing is useless, or that charging outside prices inside an airport is impossible. The video finds much closer compliance in Portland. And Portland hasn’t eliminated airport operating costs. Its 2024 convenience retail lease package combined street pricing with rent tiers of 18% to 22% of sales for locations past security, a separate 1% delivery fee, metered utilities and storage charges. And caps can restrain prices even when they’re imperfect. In February I covered a comparison of Starbucks prices across 24 airports: a grande coffee was $3 in Salt Lake City and $5.05 in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles. Phoenix had dropped its street pricing requirement. That snapshot doesn’t isolate the effect of the rules (Los Angeles had a cap and was still expensive), but it certainly doesn’t suggest that removing limits makes airport coffee cheap. I’d much rather airports were honest about the bargain: we charge merchants for access to you, operating here costs more, and the revenue helps pay for the airport and can reduce airline costs. Most major U.S. airports are publicly owned. The politicians responsible don’t want to put their names on that message. So we get a promise of street pricing, an expansive definition of the street, and an employee benefits fee at the self-checkout. And then the politicians act shocked. Shocked! When consumers face high prices. Topics on this pageAirportConcessionPrice gougingRetailChicagoDallas Fort Worth International AirportDenverHudson GroupJohn F. Nor is expensive rent entirely an outside force the airport suffers from. The airport is the landlord. It’s choosing how much revenue to extract, what operating conditions to impose, and which merchants get access to the passengers. Many airports impose even higher wage costs than the market would require on its own. That costs money, too. But since U.S. airports are predominanelty owned by government, there’s political pressure to claim that passengers are being protected from the high prices that result from the government airport’s own policies. Airports Even Approve Fees To Get Around Their Own Caps Sometimes there’s no need to fudge price comparisons to support higher pricing needed to cover an airport’s higher cost environment. The airport passes a rule to allow vendors to charge more on top of the allowed price. I’ve covered airports allowing surcharges alongside their street pricing rules. The Port Authority’s current regulation permits a separate employee wage and benefit fee of up to 3%, on top of its street price plus 15% rule. (And that ‘wage and benefit fee’ doesn’t actually go to workers as such.) Earlier this month I covered a JFK self-checkout purchase of a $21.99 book carrying a 3% employee retention fee. I’ve also covered Minneapolis’s earlier 4.5% hospitality surcharge, with a sign explaining that it isn’t a tip: Then there’s the tip screen. In Austin, I couldn’t pay by card at self-checkout for a bottle of water without entering at least a penny as a tip. Zero wasn’t an option, and entering a tip manually rejected $0. A separate Austin self-checkout I flagged in January defaulted to 18% while adding a card processing surcharge. Portland Demonstrates The Rules Can Work When The Whole Deal Works None of this means street pricing is useless, or that charging outside prices inside an airport is impossible. The video finds much closer compliance in Portland. And Portland hasn’t eliminated airport operating costs. Its 2024 convenience retail lease package combined street pricing with rent tiers of 18% to 22% of sales for locations past security, a separate 1% delivery fee, metered utilities and storage charges. And caps can restrain prices even when they’re imperfect. In February I covered a comparison of Starbucks prices across 24 airports: a grande coffee was $3 in Salt Lake City and $5.05 in Phoenix, Las Vegas and Los Angeles. Phoenix had dropped its street pricing requirement. That snapshot doesn’t isolate the effect of the rules (Los Angeles had a cap and was still expensive), but it certainly doesn’t suggest that removing limits makes airport coffee cheap. I’d much rather airports were honest about the bargain: we charge merchants for access to you, operating here costs more, and the revenue helps pay for the airport and can reduce airline costs.     #111951. A Glorious Man

    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    A Glorious Man

    📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (157 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Listen closely, and you will notice that Ben Sasse uses the word “glorious” often.
    • Sources indicate that this historian by training, turnaround specialist by trade, former senator by a felt obligation, is the rare conservative undeterred by fatalism, even — especially — when staring it in the face.

    Listen closely, and you will notice that Ben Sasse uses the word “glorious” often. He uses it for the everyday goodness of Americans, the architecture of limited government they inherited, and now for his own rendezvous with God. Death by metastatic pancreatic cancer, Sasse states, is “what I need.”.

    Sources indicate that this historian by training, turnaround specialist by trade, former senator by a felt obligation, is the rare conservative undeterred by fatalism, even — especially — when staring it in the face. In wisdom tucked into a footnote in his second book, Sasse doesn’t deny that the world is a “broken place always at risk of spinning out of control.” It’s just that he finds this unruliness quieting in a way, and responds with “profound gratitude for the gifts we’ve received and consequently aims to conserve or preserve those blessings.”.

    John R. Puri is the Thomas L. Rhodes Fellow at National Review.

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    The House has a fresh lame-duck challenge: Attendance

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S.
    • Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a upcoming challenge: Attendance.
    • In a recent development, thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., pictured at the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, noted attendance is 'a great frustration.' (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    Republicans who want to accomplish as much as possible before Democrats take control of the House are confronting a upcoming challenge: Attendance.

    In a recent development, thirty-two members – 21 Republicans, 10 Democrats, and one independent – did not vote in Thursday morning’s session before members headed out of town a day early for Thanksgiving break. This, a day after House GOP leadership pulled a procedural rule vote when it was clear the vote might fall short because of GOP no-shows – and then canceled a planned Friday voting session.

    Recent findings suggest that the House has just 12 scheduled voting days left in the 119th Congress. And leaders who have at times struggled to ensure sufficient support for their agenda from the narrow majority now say they will work to make sure cases of senioritis don’t compound the problem, as both returning and nonreturning members have been part of the problem.

    It has been revealed that "Attendance is a great frustration for me right now,” House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., told reporters Thursday. “We'll be addressing that with members.".

    “We want to run through the tape and finish strong, but we can't do that unless people are present at work, so that's our challenge,” Johnson continued.

    Recent findings suggest that of 13 roll call votes in the House since the midterms, all but one has had a double-digit number of no-shows; for five of the 13, more than 30 members did not vote. The average number of members not voting has more than doubled since the midterm elections, compared to the final 13 roll call votes beforehand.

    Industry observers note that johnson has just a few more weeks before he steps out of the spotlight and Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, takes over the GOP conference as minority leader. But his members are still counting on him to get them back to Washington.

    “I think there's going to be some serious conversations over the phone, behind the scenes over the weekend,” Rep. Michael Cloud, R-Texas, said. “We all took an oath of office. We have a sworn duty to be here. We're still being paid to be here, and you have to show up and do the job.”.

    And it's not just leadership that's frustrated with their missing colleagues this week.

    “There is, no question,” Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-N.C., who narrowly won reelection, responded when asked whether there was frustration in the caucus over members' absences.

    According to recent reports, “I don't know what you do with people that don't understand the concept of duty,” Harrigan mentioned. “I mean, look, you signed up for a two-year term. You execute your two-year term, no matter what happens along the way politically. You have an obligation both to your constituency and to your country to be here, so the fact that they're not self-motivated to be here, I don't think that there's really much that you can do.”.

    Attendance has also been a bipartisan problem. A group of House Democrats, including members of leadership, faced harsh criticism from party activists for not returning to the chamber in time for a vote related to a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

    While Republican leadership grapples with the fallout from the party’s election losses earlier this month, lawmakers still face a slew of legislative items as Congress looks ahead to the holidays and a government shutdown looms.

    Many Republicans want to see a party-line defense spending bill cross the finish line, while the NDAA remains in treacherous territory and Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act has been dark for months.

    However, the frustration does not lie solely with absent House members.

    “The Senate needs to do their job,” Rep. John McGuire, R-Va., remarked. “I know we had a hard time in the midterms. History doesn't favor the party in the president's office, but we passed the Save America Act five times here. It goes over there, nothing. We've got a farm bill, nothing. We got an NDAA. We got so many things.”.

    #111949. Tech Report: Marriott’s Worst Hotel? Rated 1.6 Stars On Its Own Site—A Guest Found Radisson Signs, Stained Sheets And A Filthy Sofa

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1866 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Marriott’s Worst Hotel? Rated 1.6 Stars On Its Own Site—A Guest Found Radisson Signs, Stained Sheets And A Filthy Sofa

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1866 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Marriott’s Buena Park Grand Hotel & Suites promises “award-winning hospitality.” Guests rate it 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website.
    • I’ve written about the 1.7-star Woodlands Plaza Toledo Hotel as a contender for the worst Marriott in North America, and about the Carambola Beach Resort, Marriott’s “regret resort.” Apparently there’s more competition in the race to the bottom.
    • Under Bill Marriott, Marriott’s sine qua non was consistency.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Marriott’s Buena Park Grand Hotel & Suites promises “award-winning hospitality.” Guests rate it 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website. A reader checked in and found stained bedding and a sofa he wouldn’t sit on. I’ve written about the 1.7-star Woodlands Plaza Toledo Hotel as a contender for the worst Marriott in North America, and about the Carambola Beach Resort, Marriott’s “regret resort.” Apparently there’s more competition in the race to the bottom. Under Bill Marriott, Marriott’s sine qua non was consistency. They didn’t always promise a lot, but they delivered exactly what they promised. The point of booking a chain was knowing what you’d get. You didn’t need to investigate eeach property to find out whether it met basic standards. You knew what the brand stood for. Now I find Marriott overpromises and enforces too little, afraid of alienating owners by making them spend money. Net rooms growth has become the priority, even when the rooms undermine the reason customers choose Marriott in the first place. Here, the property isn’t even flying one of Marriott’s flags yet and presumably there will be some investment. But they aren’t making the owner do that first, before delivering their guests. They’re trading a reputation built over decades for current fee revenue. Owners pay Marriott to deliver customers. If travelers stop trusting the company’s hotels, Marriott has fewer customers to send those owners. Then the owners have little reason to keep paying Marriott. Letting bad hotels stay in the system earns fee revenue from those properties today but sacrifices the ability of the chain to earn anything in the future. The Buena Park property is expected to transition to SpringHill Suites. Here’s a guest review from a reader with Lifetime Titanium status, who found Marriott asking $144.37 for the night. He paid less through Delta’s hotel booking portal. This is what he found. Marriott wanted $140 for a 1.6-star hotel Marriott wanted $144.37 a night for the Grand Hotel & Suites in Buena Park, California, an unbranded property that guests had rated 1.6 out of 5 on Marriott’s own website. I booked it for less through Delta and found stains on the fitted sheet, red stains beneath a pillowcase and hair on a sofa I wouldn’t sit on. When you book a Marriott, you expect a Marriott. The whole point of having a hotel company’s name behind a reservation is that somebody has exercised a little judgment on your behalf. What judgment did Marriott International exercise here? The Grand is supposed to, at some point, become a SpringHill Suites by Marriott. When I arrived, I saw no Marriott signs. Some of the old signs and placards still noted Radisson. I paid $125.22 through Delta Air Lines’ hotel booking portal. With the branding up in the air, I couldn’t tell what Bonvoy benefits or points I’d receive for paying $144.37 to book directly with Marriott. Priceline would have saved me $13.25 over Delta, but I’d have missed out on the nearly 600 SkyMiles I earned. I arrived just after 2 p.m. The front desk clerk said my room was ready, but I’d have to pay $35 to check in before 3 p.m. I passed and came back a little more than an hour later. To be fair, I’d booked through a third party. Still, I gave the clerk my Bonvoy number at check-in. She never acknowledged my Lifetime Titanium Elite status or mentioned any benefits. I didn’t even get a bottle of water. The thing is, I liked the building. Its Spanish mission revival architecture was distinctive. You could also see where a restaurant and lounge had once been located. Whoever built the Grand clearly spent money on it. I suspect it was a great hotel in the early 1980s. More than four decades of neglect had, however, turned it into a dump. I booked a park-view suite with one king bed and one sofa bed. The view from my second-floor junior suite was of a parking lot and, beyond it, the main thoroughfare. At first glance, the room looked clean. Apart from the flooring and the one TV, I’d guess it had been 20 years since anything had been updated. Even the laminate flooring was peeling and torn. The toiletries in the bathroom were a mix of brands. The tub and shower had extensive patches of what looked like black mold. Then I looked at the sofa. There was hair and debris on it. One reason to book a suite is to have somewhere to sit besides the bed. That left the bed, where I found what appeared to be fluid stains on the bedding, including the fitted sheet. Under one pillowcase, the pillow protector had red stains of its own. The Grand fell well short of what I’d expect from a Quality Inn or a Ramada. I’d put it at what I expect from the nearby Motel 6. At Marriott’s rate of $144.37, staying here is highway robbery. I don’t believe for a minute this property would have made it into the chain in this condition when the Marriott family ran the company. I can imagine Bill Marriott saying, “Call us when the renovations are finished.” Arne Sorenson, the first CEO from outside the Marriott family, and his successor, Tony Capuano, ruined the brand the Marriotts built. SpringHill Suites is supposed to be one of Marriott’s better limited-service brands. It will be a long time before the Grand comes anywhere close to that standard.     I’ve written about the 1.7-star Woodlands Plaza Toledo Hotel as a contender for the worst Marriott in North America, and about the Carambola Beach Resort, Marriott’s “regret resort.” Apparently there’s more competition in the race to the bottom.

    Under Bill Marriott, Marriott’s sine qua non was consistency. They didn’t always promise a lot, but they delivered exactly what they promised. The point of booking a chain was knowing what you’d get. You didn’t need to investigate eeach property to find out whether it met basic standards. You knew what the brand stood for.

    Industry observers note that now I find Marriott overpromises and enforces too little, afraid of alienating owners by making them spend money. Net rooms growth has become the priority, even when the rooms undermine the reason customers choose Marriott in the first place. Here, the property isn’t even flying one of Marriott’s flags yet and presumably there will be some investment. But they aren’t making the owner do that first, before delivering their guests.

    Recent findings suggest that they’re trading a reputation built over decades for current fee revenue. Owners pay Marriott to deliver customers. If travelers stop trusting the company’s hotels, Marriott has fewer customers to send those owners. Then the owners have little reason to keep paying Marriott. Letting bad hotels stay in the system earns fee revenue from those properties today but sacrifices the ability of the chain to earn anything in the future.

    According to recent reports, the Buena Park property is expected to transition to SpringHill Suites. Here’s a guest review from a reader with Lifetime Titanium status, who found Marriott asking $144.37 for the night. He paid less through Delta’s hotel booking portal. This is what he found.

    #111948. How to use the Amex Platinum Oura Ring statement credit

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    How to use the Amex Platinum Oura Ring statement credit

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, one of the top premium cards, the offers many lifestyle-centered benefits and statement credits.
    • With the end of the calendar year fast approaching, now's a good time to decide whether you can use this credit before it resets.
    • Here's how this statement credit works and whether it makes sense for you.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, one of the top premium cards, the offers many lifestyle-centered benefits and statement credits. Those include several health- and fitness-centered benefits, including an Oura Ring statement credit for up to $200 per calendar year (enrollment is required).

    With the end of the calendar year fast approaching, now's a good time to decide whether you can use this credit before it resets.

    Here's how this statement credit works and whether it makes sense for you.

    One of the many lifestyle statement credits available through the is up to $200 each calendar year toward Oura Ring. Specifically, the statement credit applies to hardware purchases only and doesn't cover subscriptions. (Enrollment is required.).

    In a recent development, the Oura Ring is a wearable, health-tracking smart ring. Some key data it tracks includes:.

    Recent findings suggest that imagine an Apple Watch or Fitbit, but in ring form. Oura right now sells the Oura Ring 4 starting at $349 and the newer Oura Ring 5 starting at $399. While this statement credit won't fully cover the cost of a ring, it will get you more than halfway there.

    One notable advantage of the Oura Ring is that you don't have to charge it as often as other wearables — the Oura Ring 5 typically lasts six or more days on a full charge.

    Related: The best credit cards to maximize fitness spending.

    Using this statement credit is easy.

    Amex states that the statement credit should post within eight weeks, but some TPG staffers have seen it post within days.

    If you're trying to use this statement credit before Dec. 31, don't wait for the last minute. Amex relies on the date Oura processes the transaction, which might be a day or two after you place the order.

    This is particularly important if you order a sizing kit: The ring itself won't process and ship until you confirm your size in your Oura account. Place your order now to get things started.

    Related: Why the new Amex Platinum changes are converting me to a cardmember.

    Sources indicate that this statement credit is a more niche perk that not all cardmembers will be able to use. For starters, many people may prefer other forms of wearables. If health data doesn't interest you, this statement credit won't move the needle either.

    Industry observers note that plus, the fact that this statement credit doesn't cover the full cost of the ring may also deter some cardmembers. The out-of-pocket cost will still run you at least $149, unless you land a good sale. You'll also need to pay for an Oura Membership at $5.99 monthly or $69.99 per year.

    I hope Amex expands this statement credit to cover a subscription in the future, since it's needed to fully maximize your Oura Ring's features.

    Even if Oura Ring is of interest, you may not want to buy a upcoming one every year, meaning some years the benefit may go unused.

    If you don't think you’d use the statement credit yourself, you could gift a ring to one of your health- and fitness-minded friends or family members.

    It's also important to note that this is a shared statement credit, meaning authorized consumers do not receive their own.

    This sole statement credit shouldn't be the deciding factor on whether you add this card to your wallet, but if you can use it organically, it can help recoup some of the Platinum's $895 annual fee (see rates and fees).

    Related: Complete guide to authorized customers on the Amex Platinum Card.

    Industry observers note that the Oura Ring statement credit can be valuable for Platinum Card members who already plan to buy a fitness tracker, especially if they can stack it with a sale. However, you might find it smarter to let the statement credit go unused some or all years.

    However, it would be ideal if this statement credit were expanded in the future to cover the subscription cost, as this would make it more accessible for more cardmembers to use year after year.

    To learn more, check out our full review of the Amex Platinum Card.

    For rates and fees of the Amex Platinum, click here.

    Tech Report: Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select Review—Why American Still Wins For Credit Card Spending Toward Status

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 45 min read (8944 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~45 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog.
    • In a recent development, american Airlines has the best overall U.S.
    • Industry observers note that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] earns one Loyalty Point per eligible dollar, without a cap.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that I receive compensation for content and many links on this blog. Be aware that websites may earn compensation when a customer clicks on a link, when an application is approved, or when an account is opened. Citibank is an advertising partner of this site, as is American Express, Chase, Capital One, and others. Any opinions expressed in this post are my own, and have not been reviewed, approved, or endorsed by my advertising partners. I do not write about all offers that are available -- instead focusing on miles, points, and cash back (and currencies that can be converted into the same). Terms apply to the offers and benefits listed on this page.

    In a recent development, american Airlines has the best overall U.S. program for making credit card spending count toward status, and you don’t need one of its expensive premium cards to take advantage of it.

    Industry observers note that the Citi® / AAdvantage® Platinum Select® World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] earns one Loyalty Point per eligible dollar, without a cap. You can combine those points with what you earn flying, shopping and through many of American’s other partners, all the way up to Executive Platinum. Meanwhile, the card’s checked bag benefit can cover its annual fee on a single family trip.

    I recently covered the card’s refresh, which adds Walmart+, an inflight credit and travel protections while raising the annual fee. Those changes take effect January 24, 2027. They improve the card for some customers, but the reason to put spending on it remains earning status.

    It has been revealed that american’s current offer is 50,000 bonus miles after $2,500 in purchases within the first three months. There’s no annual fee for the first 12 months then $99, increasing to $150 with renewals starting January 24, 2027. That means for new applications, after the introductory year, the card’s annual fee is $150. Citi’s initial bonus restriction looks back 48 months. You aren’t eligible if you’ve received a Platinum Select new account bonus during that period, or converted another Citi card on which you earned a new account bonus during that period into a Platinum Select. A bonus on a different American Airlines card doesn’t, by itself, disqualify you. The miles are worth having. I’ve written about American’s partner award sweet spots, like 70,000 miles for business class between North America and the Middle East or Indian Subcontinent. And I find the miles useful for domestic travel too, often uncovering good mileage deals when cash prices are high (my sense that American doesn’t want to discount the fare, but doesn’t expect to fill the plane without doing so). Why American Is Best Overall For Spending Toward Status The card earns one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible purchases. There’s no annual cap on that earning and no minimum flight requirement to qualify for American’s published status levels. Here are the thresholds, and the spending that would reach them if you earned nothing from flights, partners or separate Loyalty Point bonuses: AAdvantage Status   Loyalty Points   Card Spending Alone Gold   40,000   $40,000 Platinum   75,000   $75,000 Platinum Pro   125,000   $125,000 Executive Platinum   200,000   $200,000 American’s qualification year runs March 1 through the last day of February.If flights and other activity get you to 110,000 Loyalty Points, another $15,000 in eligible card purchases gets you to Platinum Pro. You can fill the gap with expenses you were going to incur anyway. The same Loyalty Points also move you toward Loyalty Point Rewards, including opportunities to select systemwide upgrades. Compare this with the UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees), which earns one Premier qualifying point per $20 and caps that earning at 1,000 points annually. That’s only part of the 6,000 points needed for United’s points-based Silver qualification path, which also requires at least four United or United Express flights. The similarly priced Platinum Select can take you all the way to American’s top published tier. Even Delta’s premium Reserve card takes $255,000 in purchases to earn Diamond through spending plus that one card’s annual head start. That’s 28,000 qualifying dollars, less the card’s 2,500-dollar head start, earned at one qualifying dollar per $10 spent. American’s $200,000 Executive Platinum threshold is available on this much less expensive card. Alaska’s Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card ($395 annual fee) earns one status point per $2, without a cap, plus 10,000 status points annually beginning with the first anniversary. It can require less spending for particular tiers. American is my overall pick because of the combination of inexpensive cards, uncapped earning, and the ability to combine spending with so many other sources of status credit. What You Earn On Purchases The January refresh expands the bonus categories: Eligible Purchases   Today   From January 24, 2027 American Airlines, restaurants and gas stations   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings through their respective sites   1 mile per dollar   3 miles per dollar Electric vehicle charging, select streaming services, and eligible rides and rail purchases   1 mile per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar Two miles per dollar on American Airlines tickets still doesn’t impress me. The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95. If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status. Free Checked Bags Can Pay For The Card The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation get their first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries. American at the moment charges $45 online or $50 at the airport for the first checked bag on a standard domestic ticket. Basic economy costs $5 more. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized users can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. Holding an eligible AAdvantage card also keeps the miles in the primary cardmember’s account from expiring. What The January Refresh Adds The annual fee rises $51. Key incremental benefits are: Walmart+ annual membership. The primary cardmember gets the $98 annual proposal, including delivery benefits, fuel savings and a streaming choice. Someone already paying for it can come out ahead from this benefit alone. Up to $100 in annual inflight credits. Eligible food, drinks and Wi-Fi purchases qualify; Admirals Club purchases don’t. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to New York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. These protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. The $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after issue and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee. This replaces the existing 25% food and beverage rebate. Half off an annual FOX One subscription. I’d assign this value only if it’s something you already want to buy. The inflight credit is better than the old rebate for someone making a modest amount of purchases. Spend $100 on eligible food and drinks and you’d receive $100 back instead of $25. The added travel protections may be more useful than the subscription benefits. Trip delay: Up to $500 per covered traveler for eligible expenses after a covered delay of at least six hours. Paying just the taxes on an AAdvantage award doesn’t limit reimbursement to that small cash payment. Trip cancellation and interruption: Coverage is limited to the lesser of $5,000 per trip or the covered amount paid with the card and/or AAdvantage miles. Lost baggage: Up to $3,000 per covered traveler, with a $10,000 total per trip; a lower per-bag limit applies to New York residents. Rental cars: Up to $75,000 for covered damage, for eligible rentals up to 31 days. Coverage is secondary in the U.S. and primary outside it. These protections begin with the refresh. Required payment methods and covered reasons differ by benefit. The card also retains up to $180 in Turo credits per calendar year, limited to $30 per eligible completed trip. You need six rentals to use the full amount, must link the card to your Turo account, and need to pay directly with it rather than through a digital wallet. There’s also 10% off eligible American Airlines Vacations packages. The $20,000 Spending Bonus Is Useful, But Do The Math Currently, spending $20,000 during your cardmembership year and renewing the card earns a $125 American Airlines Flight Discount. The refresh increases that to $150. The new discount adds 0.75% of the $20,000 in spending, assuming you use its full value. The increase itself is only another 0.125%. This isn’t an automatic annual flight credit just for holding the card. Under the published terms, the certificate expires one year after issue and can’t pay award-ticket taxes. Your cardmembership year also isn’t necessarily the same as the March-to-February status year. I’d count this as an extra return if I were already putting $20,000 on the card for Loyalty Points. I’d also consider moving a little spending to finish the threshold if I were close. I wouldn’t move $20,000 away from much better earning elsewhere simply because the flight discount happens to match the annual fee. Which American Airlines Card Should You Have? Platinum Select doesn’t include Admirals Club access or a general discount on award redemptions. The higher fee and extra benefits don’t change that. For an occasional American Airlines flyer without status, I’d choose it when checked bag savings and benefits I’d actually use cover the renewal fee. The first year’s $0 annual fee and initial bonus make trying it particularly easy. For someone who already has status, or another American Airlines card, I’d compare these options: Citi® / AAdvantage® Globe™ Mastercard® [See rates and fees] The $350 annual fee buys four Admirals Club Globe passes each calendar year, among other benefits. More interesting to me, the Flight Streak Bonus earns 5,000 additional Loyalty Points after every four qualifying American Airlines flight segments, up to 15,000 per qualification year. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee.     Industry observers note that the card earns one Loyalty Point per dollar of eligible purchases. There’s no annual cap on that earning and no minimum flight requirement to qualify for American’s published status levels.

    Here are the thresholds, and the spending that would reach them if you earned nothing from flights, partners or separate Loyalty Point bonuses:.

    American’s qualification year runs March 1 through the last day of February.If flights and other activity get you to 110,000 Loyalty Points, another $15,000 in eligible card purchases gets you to Platinum Pro. You can fill the gap with expenses you were going to incur anyway.

    The same Loyalty Points also move you toward Loyalty Point Rewards, including opportunities to select systemwide upgrades.

    Compare this with the UnitedSM Explorer Card (See rates and fees), which earns one Premier qualifying point per $20 and caps that earning at 1,000 points annually. That’s only part of the 6,000 points needed for United’s points-based Silver qualification path, which also requires at least four United or United Express flights. The similarly priced Platinum Select can take you all the way to American’s top published tier.

    According to recent reports, even Delta’s premium Reserve card takes $255,000 in purchases to earn Diamond through spending plus that one card’s annual head start. That’s 28,000 qualifying dollars, less the card’s 2,500-dollar head start, earned at one qualifying dollar per $10 spent. American’s $200,000 Executive Platinum threshold is available on this much less expensive card.

    In a recent development, alaska’s Atmos™ Rewards Summit Visa Infinite® credit card ($395 annual fee) earns one status point per $2, without a cap, plus 10,000 status points annually beginning with the first anniversary. It can require less spending for particular tiers. American is my overall pick because of the combination of inexpensive cards, uncapped earning, and the ability to combine spending with so many other sources of status credit.

    It has been revealed that the January refresh expands the bonus categories: Eligible Purchases   Today   From January 24, 2027 American Airlines, restaurants and gas stations   2 miles per dollar   2 miles per dollar AAdvantage Hotels and AAdvantage Cars bookings through their respective sites   1 mile per dollar   3 miles per dollar Electric vehicle charging, select streaming services, and eligible rides and rail purchases   1 mile per dollar   2 miles per dollar Other purchases   1 mile per dollar   1 mile per dollar Two miles per dollar on American Airlines tickets still doesn’t impress me. The Citi Strata Premier® Card (See rates and fees.) earns three points per dollar on airfare, hotels, restaurants, supermarkets, gas and electric vehicle charging. Its points transfer to American, and its annual fee is $95. If I just wanted redeemable American miles, I’d generally prefer Strata Premier for those categories. The value in spending on this card is progress towards AAdvantage status. Free Checked Bags Can Pay For The Card The primary cardmember and up to four companions on the same reservation get their first checked bag free on eligible domestic American Airlines itineraries. American right now charges $45 online or $50 at the airport for the first checked bag on a standard domestic ticket. Basic economy costs $5 more. For two people each checking one bag on a domestic roundtrip, the savings are $180 compared with paying the standard fee online. That’s already more than the coming $150 annual fee. A family of four doing the same saves $360. You don’t have to buy the tickets with this card to receive the bag benefit. Your AAdvantage number needs to be on the reservation. The whole itinerary must qualify as domestic American Airlines or American Eagle travel. The primary cardmember must travel. An authorized user doesn’t get an independent bag allowance when traveling alone. If your status or cabin already includes a free bag, holding the card doesn’t add another one. You also get Group 5 preferred boarding, including up to four companions on the same reservation. That puts you ahead of later economy groups and improves your chances of finding overhead bin space. There are no foreign transaction fees, and authorized people can be added without an additional annual fee. Their spending earns miles and Loyalty Points for the primary cardmember. You don’t need to put spending on Globe to earn that flight bonus. Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] At a $695 annual fee, this is the card for an Admirals Club membership. It also awards 10,000 bonus Loyalty Points when you reach each of 50,000, 90,000, 165,000 and 240,000 Loyalty Points in a qualification year. Those thresholds can be reached through flights, partners or spending on other American Airlines cards. Citi® / AAdvantage BusinessTM World Elite Mastercard® [See rates and fees] Business owners should compare its separate initial bonus and spending benefits. Through December 31, 2028, eligible employee-card spending earns a Loyalty Point per dollar for the employee and an additional Loyalty Point for the primary cardmember. That’s status credit for two people from the same spending, rather than two points for one person. For instance, someone holding Executive can put dining and gas purchases on Platinum Select for two miles per dollar, earn the same basic Loyalty Point per dollar, and still trigger Executive’s account-wide Loyalty Point bonuses. They’d need enough value from Platinum Select’s extra miles, benefits and flight discount to justify its separate annual fee.     I will not be playing Grand Theft Auto VI. The limited flexibility left in my wrists after decades of typing and mousing and gaming must be reserved for a game I started three years ago and haven’t finished. I’m stuck in a shed in the rain, low on ammo, and there is a big Nazi robot outside. I have to find the time and desire to return to this dangerous situation and beat the robot before the red bar over my head that reads CARPAL TUNNEL goes fully red. But the main reason I won’t play GTA: I don’t wish to inhabit the life of an uninhibited sociopath.

    Nor do I need a girlfriend. Rob Henderson, in The Spectator, notes:.

    #111945. Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    Appeals court stands by LaMonica McIver ruling

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December.
    • LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.
    • Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., is seen on Capitol Hill last December. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    According to recent reports, rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., faced a setback Thursday in her effort to ditch charges tied to a scuffle during an oversight visit at an immigration detention facility last year, as a federal appeals court declined to reconsider its decision to let the case move forward.

    The decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit leaves in place a 2-1 opinion from August which held that McIver was not immune from the charges, which stemmed from a confrontation between visiting members of Congress and federal agents while at the Delaney Hall facility in Newark. McIver has challenged the charges, arguing that her visit fell under the “speech or debate” immunity she has as a member of Congress because she was there to inspect detention conditions.

    In a statement McIver said she and her attorneys were looking at “every possible option” in response to the appeals court ruling. Her statement invoked the Trump administration’s threats to treat oversight efforts as criminal conduct and said “we are all one step closer to a world in which the president of the United States can try to imprison people simply because he does not like what they stand for.”.

    Recent findings suggest that “Donald Trump continues to send warning shots to Democrats in Congress and in all levels of power — but their case against me right now, in broad daylight, goes well beyond a warning. Because of a weaponized Department of Justice and because I dared to do my job and conduct oversight of ICE, I am facing 17 years in prison,” McIver remarked in her statement.

    Following Thursday’s decision on rehearing, McIver could next ask the Supreme Court to weigh in on the case.

    In a recent development, the August majority opinion from Judge Cindy Chung, which Thursday’s decision leaves in place, stated that two of the three charges against McIver did not fall under the immunity, which is limited to legislative acts. The majority sent the third charge back to the lower court for another ruling.

    “We have considered the ‘nature’ of the charged conduct and concluded it is unambiguously non-legislative,” the judge wrote.

    Separately, Judge Thomas Ambro partially dissented to offer a different approach to the case. Ambro would have required the trial judge to more closely examine the exact conduct McIver was charged with, as well as to examine whether the Trump administration targeted her because of her political views.

    “I would allow her discovery into the truth of the matter — not only for her own sake but to safeguard the independence of our legislative bodies,” Ambro wrote.

    Ambro did not vote on whether the full 3rd Circuit should rehear the case. Three judges voted to have the full 3rd Circuit hear McIver’s case, and Judge Emil Bove, a former Trump administration official and former personal attorney for the president, did not participate in the vote.

    Sources indicate that the criminal case started shortly after the Delaney Hall visit in May 2025, as prosecutors alleged that McIver assaulted federal agents during a scuffle around Newark Mayor Ras Baraka. Officials arrested Baraka that day and charged him with trespassing, but later dropped those charges.

    According to recent reports, court filings in the case alleged that McIver struck agents during the confrontation. McIver has argued that she was effectively being charged for doing her job and federal agents were interfering with her attempts to inspect the facility.

    Sources indicate that earlier this year, Judge Jamel K. Semper of the U.S. District Court for the District of New Jersey disagreed and ruled that the case could move forward.

    First Look Inside American Airlines’ New Austin Lounge—Twice The Space, An Outdoor Terrace And Skyline Views

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that I finally got inside American Airlines’ new Austin airport lounge this week.
    • In a recent development, american Airlines should be opening its Newly introduced York JFK ‘Provisions’ grab ‘n go lounge for Admirals Club members in the next month, complete with barista bar.
    • By the end of next year we should also see the newly introduced Austin Admiral’s Club as well.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that I finally got inside American Airlines’ new Austin airport lounge this week. It’s still a shell, but the covered outdoor terrace is already there, and you can see the downtown skyline from the west end of the lounge. The new Admirals Club will have more than twice the space of the current one, and Austin is just one of the places where American is building bigger lounges. American Airlines should be opening its New York JFK ‘Provisions’ grab ‘n go lounge for Admirals Club members in the next month, complete with barista bar. And we’ll see both the renovated Washington National D concourse and replacement Chicago O’Hare L concourse clubs next year. By the end of next year we should also see the new Austin Admiral’s Club as well. The core and shell space is about to be turned over to American by the airport, allowing them to begin construction work. The current club is small. It was perfect-sized when I moved to Austin, but Austin has grown and overall American Airlines lounge visits have increased 80% over the past decade. Expectations for food have increased, too, and the kitchen facilities are inadequate. American is replacing its current club with a new one at the west end of the airport’s main concourse. In March, American Airlines announced the details of the plan for the new club above gate 35. More than 12,000 square feet (more than double the size of the current club) With an outdoor terrace and views of both downtown and airport operations. Supporting a gate allocation that’s expected to nearly double when the new terminal opens in the early 2030s. I keep looking at the space, waiting for progress, each time I fly out of the airport. I’m anxious for the new lounge! So far there are two renderings of the space that have been made available: Credit: American Airlines Credit: American Airlines This week I had a chance to peek inside the space, see the actual views from the space and the outdoor terrace. When you come up the elevator or walk up the stairs you’ll see the entrance – they’ll be taking down a preexisting wall there, and will install e-gates which are a new club standard (like at the Philadelphia A-West club – that location also has e-gates for the Flagship business class lounge, but that won’t be a standard). The kitchen will be at the far left, back of the lounge when you enter. The full kitchen facilities will allow in-house preparation for upgraded food. Closer, also to the left but nearer the windows will be the bar. At the opposite (west) end of the lounge, you can see out towards the downtown skyline. It gives some perspective on how small Austin’s downtown really is, though it’s far more dense than it was when I first moved here. The lounge’s outdoor deck has covering and shade, and American tells me it will have misters and fans – making it much more usable throughout the year. Living in Austin we eat outdoors much of the year, though the summers can get very hot and there will be days you don’t want to be outdoors between November and February. The former Chase Terrace on the opposite end of the airport lacked covering and climate assistance. Taking photos from the lounge is a bit challenging, because of the screens that the airport installs on the window meant for birds to be able to identify the glass and not fly into the building. Nonetheless, angle the lens just right and zoom past it and your photos can come closer to what you see out the windows (you really don’t see these screens except when you’re up close to the glass). American’s Austin gate allocation goes from 4 to 9 — a 125% increase – when the new concourse opens in the early 2030s. American can use common use gates in addition today. All nine of their dedicated gates will be on the current concourse, near this new lounge. Austin is part of a larger investment American is now making in its clubs. After several years where there wasn’t any growth in its network, and they even closed some lounges, here’s the American Airlines lounge pipeline: Airport Project Timing / status Austin New Admirals Club above the west gate expansion: more than 12,000 square feet, roughly double the current club, with an outdoor terrace. Permits issued, but American hasn’t announced an opening date. Expected at the end of 2027. Charlotte New Admirals Club above the airport atrium: more than 40,000 square feet, with showers, multiple bars and food stations. 2028 anticipated. Charlotte First Flagship Lounge, separately announced from the new Admirals Club. Size and opening date haven’t been disclosed. Chicago O’Hare Replacement Concourse L Admirals Club exceeding 10,000 square feet, with more seating and airfield views. Construction underway. Existing L club stays open during the work. No opening date announced. Dallas–Fort Worth New Terminal C Admirals Club: 37,000 square feet near the Skylink station. No opening date disclosed. Dallas–Fort Worth Terminal F Provisions by Admirals Club, the initial lounge offering in a broader premium-space program for the new terminal. Planned for Terminal F’s first phase. Later premium spaces and individual opening dates haven’t been shared. Miami New Flagship Lounge and expanded D30 Admirals Club. The current Flagship space becomes Admirals Club space, nearly doubling American’s total lounge footprint at the airport. No opening date disclosed. Nashville Replacement Admirals Club in the new Concourse A: about 17,400 square feet including outdoor terraces and an interior balcony, replacing the current roughly 7,000 square foot club. Construction expected to begin in 2027. No firm opening date announced. New York JFK Provisions by Admirals Club in Terminal 8: 3,700 square feet near gates 12–14, with hot and cold food, a dedicated barista bar and customer assistance. Targeted for December 2026. Phoenix Expansion and refresh of all three Terminal 4 Admirals Clubs. Near term work at A19–A21 improves food service. The B5–B7 club gets 20% more seats. Longer term, the two A clubs nearly triple their combined space and add approximately 150% more seats. Announced November 2026. No completion dates disclosed. San Antonio First Admirals Club in new Terminal C. Airport aims specify a 10,000 square foot American Airlines lounge. Documented by the airport, no formal American lounge announcement yet. Terminal C targets mid-2028, but no separate lounge opening date. Washington National Rebuilt Concourse D Admirals Club: more than 10,000 square feet and approximately 50% more seats. Expected to deliver in 2027. The real treat in Austin, though, isn’t the design or that there will be an outdoor deck – it’s the staff in the Austin club who are the absolute best in the system. They know the names of all regulars on sight and welcome you into the lounge. They work magic with itineraries – and they keep working that magic even once you’ve left, frequently bird dogging inventory and improving connections even after you’ve left the lounge. When I’ve had flights cancelled and could only get a long connection in Dallas or Charlotte, I’ve found myself landing to notes saying they’ve gotten me on an earlier flight because space opened up. They do this for everyone. It’s a small city, personal customer service feel even in a growing market. And that makes Admirals Club membership (and Citi® / AAdvantage® Executive World Legend Mastercard® [See rates and fees] cardmembership) worth it. The Austin club space will finally match the service once this lounge opens. I genuinely cannot wait for the lounge to open because it’ll make flying American Airlines out of my home airport that much better.     With Huang Return, Trump Backs Silicon Valley's Founder Mode

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (291 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Realclearpolitics

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Click below to continue reading this story, discover more Markets stories from over 25 years of RealClear archives, or follow this topic to stay in the know.
    • Recent findings suggest that NYU economist Scott Galloway, who predicted last week there was "almost zero chance" Jensen Huang would be reinstated as Nvidia CEO, doubled down on his criticism following Huang's return.
    • Recent findings suggest that reason has prevailed, as has economic literacy with the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Click below to continue reading this story, discover more Markets stories from over 25 years of RealClear archives, or follow this topic to stay in the know.

    Ryanair Flew 208 Million Passengers At An Average Fare Of $56—Now Its Rivals Want It Grounded For Not Being European Enough

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2612 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that A trade group representing Lufthansa, Air France and KLM has gone to court in Ireland to challenge Ryanair’s right to fly.
    • According to recent reports, european investors hold just 30% of Ryanair’s shares.
    • The European Network Airlines Association notes it asked the European Commission and national regulators to check Ryanair’s ownership after the airline loosened its share purchase rules.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that A trade group representing Lufthansa, Air France and KLM has gone to court in Ireland to challenge Ryanair’s right to fly. Their objection is to who owns the airline that carried 208 million passengers at an average fare of just €51 in the year ended March 31. European investors hold just 30% of Ryanair’s shares. Competitors say they run afoul of foreign ownership rules, but those European investors exercise 100% voting control of the ariline. I don’t see Europe grounding Ryanair. I do see why its competitors might like want to pick this fight. The European Network Airlines Association notes it asked the European Commission and national regulators to check Ryanair’s ownership after the airline loosened its share purchase rules. That didn’t get them what they wanted so they sued the Irish Aviation Authority. On November 16, the judge declined to add Lufthansa, Air France and KLM as parties to the case, though they can submit affidavits. A hearing is scheduled for December 16. Who Owns Ryanair, And Who Gets Control? Brexit turned British shareholders into foreign investors without anybody having to sell a share. Since January 2021, nonqualifying shareholders haven’t been allowed to attend, speak or vote at Ryanair shareholder meetings. On March 7, 2025, Ryanair let them buy ordinary shares in Dublin again. It kept the voting ban, including for any votes the chairman might otherwise cast on their behalf. Ryanair says the change opened the door to inclusion in stock indexes. Its board said it would restrict purchases again if European ownership fell to 20%. . At both March 31 and September 30 this year, Ryanair put qualifying European ownership at 30%. That includes investors from Norway, Iceland, Liechtenstein and Switzerland. Shares held through its U.S. depositary are generally non-qualifying. Here’s who highlights up in Ryanair’s March 31 shareholder disclosure. Reported holder    Share of Ryanair Capital Group 14.6% MFS 4.7% Artisan Partners 4.5% Michael O’Leary 4.0% BlackRock 4.0% Fidelity 3.3% By October, Capital Group reported 15.70% for client accounts, and T. Rowe Price reported 3.00%. O’Leary’s 4% economic stake translates to 13% voting control. Does It Matter More Who Owns The Shares Or Who Controls The Airline? European law requires both. Qualifying states or their nationals have to own more than half the airline and effectively control it. Giving Europeans every vote solves the legal issue of control. The key legal question here is whether shares that carry no voting rights count as equity for the ownership test. European regulators have allowed this in the past. Wizz Air says British and Hungarian regulators approved its initiative to suspend some foreign shareholders’ votes after Brexit so Wizz Air Hungary could keep its European license. easyJet just did this in a takeover vote. When shareholders approved an Apollo deal on November 11, qualifying Europeans owned 35.07% of easyJet. It suspended voting rights on 233,921,894 shares. Those shareholders keep their dividend rights. The proposed deal itself caps Apollo’s ordinary equity at 49.9%. But this is complicated. A 1995 Swissair–Sabena decision found that Swissair held 49.5% of the Belgian airline’s voting shares, plus special certificates that the European Commission agreed to leave out of the ownership calculation. Those certificates had no votes, generally paid at least 5% and gave Swissair no share of the assets left over in liquidation. That looked like debt. In contrast, a Ryanair shareholder who can’t vote still collects dividends (which aren’t fixed) and gains or loses money on fluctuations of the stock. What Happens If Ryanair Loses? If all the ordinary shares count, Ryanair has to get qualifying ownership above 50%. That’s 207 million existing shares moving from non-European to European owners (assuming they don’t issue newly introduced shares). The airline’s articles of incorporation allow it to direct restricted holders to sell to qualifying investors. This is being framed in some quarters as Ryanair having to shut down. That doesn’t seem likely. I’ve been writing about foreign airline ownership since 2003. If someone abroad is willing to put up the money for more planes and cheaper flights, what does the passenger gain by turning them away? If Europe needs aircraft and crews available for defense, it can pay airlines to provide them. Forcing a British retiree to sell Ryanair stock to a Frenchman doesn’t add aircraft that Europe can use for its defense. It does, however, give Lufthansa and Air France a way to raise a competitor’s cost of capital. So it’s decent return on trade association dues.
