    #111939. Industry News: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Maine senators at odds over credit for earmarks

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks.
    • After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.
    • Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Collins took sole responsibility for a larger share of Maine earmarks. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After a bruising reelection defeat, Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, is ready to play hardball.

    Eager to show how much she's delivered for her constituents, Collins took the lion's share of credit in her committee's fiscal 2027 spending bills for Maine earmarks — at the expense of her delegation colleague, independent Angus King, who caucuses with Democrats.

    The amount of earmarks King secured fell dramatically compared to his previous year's total in Senate Appropriations Committee bills, as Collins took sole credit for most earmarks both senators had requested.

    The power play has instigated a dispute over how to award credit for "congressionally directed spending," better known as earmarks. It has also raised questions about a Senate rule that requires committee leaders to disclose the name of each senator who requested projects to be included in a spending bill before it can move on the floor.

    Industry observers note that it’s undeniable that as the chair of the spending panel, Collins has more influence over which projects reach the final bills than her delegation mate. Collins spokesperson Phoebe Keller mentioned that since available earmark funding is split into separate pots for the majority and minority to dole out, the bills reflect which of those funding sources was tapped to provide money to the relevant projects.

    Keller noted that Collins deserves sole credit for the contested projects, as listed in the reports accompanying the bills.

    "When only Collins is listed, it reflects only she chose to fund the project,” Keller remarked.

    A Democratic committee aide contested that characterization, saying that traditionally all requesters are named regardless of which party’s funding allocation is tapped for a project.

    “The handling of these particular projects is a clear departure from the norm and will need to be rectified in conference negotiations,” the aide noted.

    Industry observers note that king is credited with approximately $54 million in fiscal 2027 earmarks in the bills Collins released this month, including joint projects with Collins. That's down from around $231 million in the Senate's fiscal 2026 bills, according to a CQ Roll Call analysis.

    Last year, King and Collins were both listed on 75 of the 77 projects that both requested that were included in the Senate bills, with just two carrying only Collins’ name. This year, Collins claimed sole responsibility for over $125 million in projects that both she and King requested, approximately two-thirds of the joint requests.

    While King’s overall requests fell by more than $200 million this year versus last, his success in securing requested funds plummeted at a far greater rate with less credit for overlapping projects.

    The joint requests for which Collins claimed sole credit include five for the Maine Department of Transportation in the Transportation-HUD bill, including $10.7 million for northern freight rail improvements; $9.6 million for Route 26 reconstruction in Oxford; and $7.2 million for improvements in Rockport, among others.

    In the Labor-HHS-Education bill, projects Collins took sole credit for include $4 million for the University of Maine for biology laboratory equipment and just over $4 million for the creation of a modern emergency helipad at Lincoln Hospital.

    And the Interior-Environment bill features $4 million each for wastewater improvements in Limestone and Kennebec that both Collins and King asked for but are only attributed to Collins, among others.

    Similarly, the Agriculture, Commerce-Justice-Science and Homeland Security bills all include a project requested by both senators that only Collins is listed as securing in the bill.

    The outgoing Appropriations chair’s ability to fuel billions of dollars in federal funding for her state during her career was the centerpiece of her ultimately unsuccessful campaign for reelection, which she lost to Democrat Troy Jackson.

    As written, the draft bills appear to risk running afoul of a Senate rule that requires the committee’s chair to identify each senator who requested projects in a bill online at least 48 hours before a vote to advance the legislation on the floor.

    The relevant rule, Senate Rule 44, states that it is out of order to vote on a motion to proceed to consider a bill unless the chairman of the committee certifies that “each congressionally directed spending item . . . has been identified through lists, charts, or other similar means including the name of each Senator who submitted a request to the committee for each item so identified.”.

    That information must be “available on a publicly accessible congressional website in a searchable format at least 48 hours before such vote.”.

    A King spokesman called on the spending panel to add his name to the relevant requests.

    “We believe this must have been an oversight and assume the committee will update the requests —per Senate rules — once it’s called to their attention,” King spokesman Matthew Felling noted.

    Industry observers note that the bills released by Collins are drafts, and no floor action on final fiscal 2027 spending bills is expected this Congress. There’s limited time left before the Dec. 11 spending deadline, when all current funding is set to expire, and Democrats want to wait to negotiate final bills until they retake majorities in both chambers next year.

    But to comply with the rule, before the bills reach the floor the reports accompanying the bills, that includes the earmark tables, may have to be rewritten to list King on the contested projects, or the committee may need to disclose the information elsewhere online.

    Both chambers unveiled stricter ethics guidelines surrounding earmarks in 2021 when the practice returned after a decade-long ban.

    Peter Cohn contributed to this report.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Delta Air Lines flight attendants could be on the cusp of unionizing, but creating a union may be a card best kept in reserve – rather than one they should actually play.
    • AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson states she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines.
    • Nelson told Sumers she’s close to the union’s private target, which is above 50%.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Delta Air Lines flight attendants could be on the cusp of unionizing, but creating a union may be a card best kept in reserve – rather than one they should actually play. It can be a useful stalking horse, where the airline pays up generously to keep its crew from unionizing. But once they actually pull the trigger, there’s little reason – or ability – to continue paying above industry wages. AFA-CWA union head Sara Nelson claims she’s close to the card count her union wants before asking for a vote at Delta Air Lines. Brian Sumers came away from their November 12 interview at the Skift Aviation Forum thinking she’ll get an election and win it. A vote in 2027 is a real possibility. If I were Delta crew I’d vote no. The union would get about 30,000 flight attendants to represent. Crews who already get better than what other airline unions bargain for could wind up taking home less. Nelson told Sumers she’s close to the union’s private target, which is above 50%. The National Mediation Board needs valid cards from at least half the eligible flight attendants, and a card more than a year old won’t count. Delta organizers put the minimum at roughly 15,000 signatures. Once there’s an election, a majority of valid votes cast decides it. Nelson also said she was months away in 2024. Later that November organizers said they were weeks from having the cards. Delta flight attendants have rejected representation three times, but the vote after the Northwest merger was close. In 2010, 9,544 voted against representation and 9,216 voted for it. Sumers says he hears more confidence from Nelson this time. She can pick when to file, and a loss would normally mean waiting a year to try again while cards expire. If Nelson files with a comfortable cushion above the threshold, that would give her the edge in an election. Delta’s Pay Advantage Is Profit Sharing American Airlines and United Airlines now pay slightly higher hourly rates at the top of the flight pay scale. It’s $86.32 per flight hour at Delta, $87.04 at American and $87.47 at United. At 80 flight hours a month, United’s $1.15 advantage is about $1,100 a year in base pay.For newer hires, Delta starts a little higher than both. But Delta flight attendants actually make quite a bit more. Delta paid out $1.3 billion in February for 2025, or 8.9% of eligible earnings. United recorded $704 million for profit sharing and associated payroll taxes for the same year. Delta calculates that a flight attendant working 80 flight hours a month makes $5,100 more than United for a upcoming hire and $6,200 at the top of the scale, including United’s retro pay attributable to 2026. United got boarding pay in its new deal. It kept a its inferior profit sharing formula. Delta puts 10% of the first $2.5 billion of eligible pretax profit into the pool and 20% above that. At United, the 20% rate kicks in only on earnings above the previous year’s. American negotiated the Delta thresholds and still has much smaller checks because American Airlines doesn’t make money. . The Delta campaign’s website still lists $50 a month in dues and says they’d start after flight attendants ratify a first contract. The union’s board raised the standard rate to $65.36 in June so Delta’s cabin crew are being sold a lower cost than they’d actually face. That’s $784 a year, or about $23.5 million in gross annual dues from 30,000 flight attendants. Union Flight Attendants Go A Long Time Between Raises Delta gave its flight attendants a 4% raise in June, its fifth annual increase in a row (there was a pause for the depths of the pandemic, when Delta didn’t furlough anyone while unionized American and United furloughed tens of thousands). United’s old wage table last went up in 2020. The contract became amendable in August 2021, and the next general raise took effect May 31, 2026 with the new contract. Consumer prices went up about 29% between September 2020 and May 2026. A senior United flight attendant was still on $67.11 per flight hour just before the new deal. It took more than $86 by then just to buy what $67.11 did in 2020. Airline labor contracts become amendable and the old terms generally stay in force while the parties bargain. The National Mediation Board can release the parties from mediation, normally starting a 30 day cooling off period before the union can strike or the airline can impose new terms. In practice that hasn’t happened for flight attendants since 1993. Nelson said at Skift that she wants more frequent bargaining to deliver smaller, more regular raises. Why It Took So Long To Pay For Boarding Delta started paying for scheduled boarding time in 2022 at half the flight hourly rate. I wrote then that the organizing drive probably helped get it done. American added boarding pay in 2024 and United now uses the same half-rate approach as Delta. At Hawaiian Airlines, the same union asked for boarding pay and came away without it in its 2025 extension. AFA-CWA hadn’t gotten it at Spirit, either. There’s a reason boarding pay is a bigger deal to junior crew. Fly three short flights and you board three airplanes. Fly one long trip with the same flight hours and you board once. If the airline’s putting a limited amount of money on the table, the senior flight attendant who can bid the long trips generally does better with a higher flight rate. A junior flight attendant gets more out of a separate boarding premium. Both have to live with what the bargaining committee prioritizes. Boarding pay didn’t happen until non-union Delta did it because unions are often about dividing a fixed pie of spoils between members, rather than getting more from the airline. Senior crew preferred higher hourly rates, redistributing income up to them from more junior crew. Once Delta did it, though, that changed the dynamic and flight attendant unions had to re-prioritize their bargaining. What Delta And Its Crews Have To Lose I generally find Delta’s crew a little friendlier and more interested in getting the service right. Southwest Airlines has some of the friendliest flight attendants in the business and they’re unionized. Southwest has always hired for the right attitude. At Delta, part of the advantage comes from being able to change how the cabin runs and reward the people doing the work. The union’s first contract policy calls for writing existing work rules into a contract. If new rules make it harder to run the operation or deliver service that passengers pay extra for, Delta has less money and profit sharing falls. Bear in mind also that while the union says they protect workers from management, sometimes it’s the union that a flight attendant needs protection from. I covered United firing two union representatives after the airline concluded they’d solicited false complaints against a flight attendant who raised a safety concern. The union sued over United’s investigation of the reps and a federal judge dismissed its suit. At Southwest, four flight attendants faced internal charges for allegedly trying to replace their union. Another flight attendant won $1 million after the union got the airline to fire her. Alaska Airlines flight attendants, meanwhile, have been suing saying that the union pushed htem out over their Christianity and views on LGBT rights. If Delta flight attendants vote down a first contract, they’re still stuck with the union. If union leaders don’t follow the wishes of flight attendants, they’re still stuck with the union (and they don’t actually have direct say in how the parent union is governed). To go back to representing themselves, they’d normally have to wait two years from certification, get valid cards from at least half the workgroup and then win another election. Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement. At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers. Union organizers at Delta pitch that they’d take current pay, benefits and work rules and negotiate up from there. That’s not how any of this works. The current union status and bundle they receive today is all bundled together. A union deal would be ex nihilo and more like other airlines. There are tradeoffs between their pay and work rules. Someone working at Delta might prefer a different arrangement (though they should remember why they chose Delta over others in the first place). But it’s a different arrangement. At some airlines I’d take that deal. At Delta, flight attendants already have it better than at their peers. They have better pay and a product they’re proud of. Sara Nelson wants them to give her union their money – and possibly wind up taking home less. Since it’s virtually an irreversible decision, that’s not a button I’d push. It seems like a decision to make only when things are dire, not when they’re going well relative to peers.     #111937. Tech Report: How to use AI to find the best flight deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (168 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thepointsguy ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: How to use AI to find the best flight deals

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (168 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Thepointsguy

    ⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
  • Artificial intelligence tools can now assist travelers in finding flight deals, comparing prices and deciphering fare rules, especially during major sales like Black Friday and Cyber Monday.
  • AI can help suggest alternative airports, flexible travel dates and analyze whether cash or points provide better value for booking flights.
  • Despite improvements, AI still struggles with finding real-time award availability and may present outdated or unbookable fares.
  • Combining AI with established search engines and deal-alert services yields the best results for travelers seeking savings.
  • AI-generated fares may not always reflect live prices or include all taxes and fees, so always verify before booking.
  • Award space and special promotions can vanish quickly, and AI may not capture dynamic changes or blackout dates.
  • AI is best used as a supplement to flight search tools and deal-alert platforms, not as a sole resource.

    #111936. Industry News: Woman Faced A Felony Charge For Stealing A Rental Car—Then Won A Seat In Congress And Prosecutors Dropped The Case

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 31m • 📚 Deep Dive (6150 w)
    📖 Baca
    EV & Auto ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Viewfromthewing ↗ Open Full Page

    Industry News: Woman Faced A Felony Charge For Stealing A Rental Car—Then Won A Seat In Congress And Prosecutors Dropped The Case

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 31 min read (6150 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Viewfromthewing

    ⏱️ ~31 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • This year was such a wave election that in some cases candidate quality didn’t matter at all.
    • Sources indicate that shortly before the election, Democratic congressional candidate LaKesha Womack pulled into a high school parking lot in North Carolina for a Sunday rally.
    • The incumbent congressman she was running against turned the rental into a television ad.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    This year was such a wave election that in some cases candidate quality didn’t matter at all. It was enough to win just not to be a Republican. Shortly before the election, Democratic congressional candidate LaKesha Womack pulled into a high school parking lot in North Carolina for a Sunday rally. A sheriff’s deputy pulled up behind her. He handed her a felony summons for stealing a Toyota Corolla she’d rented from Budget nearly seven years earlier. The incumbent congressman she was running against turned the rental into a television ad. She won anyway. And on Tuesday, after Budget got paid for the six weeks its car was overdue, the district attorney dropped the charge for good. It’s good to get elected to Congress. Budget Car Rental Got The Corolla Back In 2019 Womack picked up the car in Charlotte on August 27, 2019, and renewed the rental twice. Her last extension began October 7, 2019. According to the police report the vehicle was due back at noon on October 23. On November 26 an officer reported that police couldn’t find her and put out an all points bulletin. Police recovered the Corolla and returned it to Budget on December 4, 42 days late. Budget sold the vehicle the following year. Womack has a number of excuses for never returning the car. She notes a diabetic seizure and long hospitalization had wiped her out financially. (It’s not clear why that kept her from returning it.) Her son went into foster care while she was in the hospital (again, unclear why that kept her from returning it) and the two of them wound up living in a hotel (hotels have parking, but the hotel didn’t force her to keep the car). She’d expected the manufacturer to come get the car. She says she had nowhere reliable to receive mail (when you rent a car you know you’re supposed to give it back, even without a mailed notice) and she thought the matter was settled (exactly how it would have been is unclear). On January 14, 2020, a court issued a summons for felony failure to return the car. Under North Carolina law, willfully keeping a rental vehicle past its deadline is a felony if the vehicle is worth more than $4,000. The car was valued at $20,000. Womack says she first heard about the case on Friday, October 9, 2026. A local reporter posted the records. She responded, “I do owe them people some money, obviously.” BREAKING: Documents pulled from the NC Courts government website show District 14 congressional candidate Lakesha Womack has a “pending” felony warrant for failure to return a rental car in 2019. Police records say Budget Car Rental rented a car to Womack on Oct. 7, 2019 and it was supposed be returned on Oct 23, 2019. Pics and links attached. https://t.co/4WZRvweFxM — Brett Jensen WBT News (@Brett_Jensen) October 9, 2026 Two days later, on October 11, the summons was reissued. A Polk County deputy’s body camera caught the handoff outside the county Democratic rally. Republican Congressman Tim Moore ran an ad on this. Watch Tim Moore’s campaign ad, “Keep Your Money.” He Helped Draw The District. She Didn’t Even Live In It. Moore spent ten years as speaker of the North Carolina House, helped gerrymander the district to favor Republicans and won it in 2024 by nearly 65,000 votes. Womack, an ordained minister making her first run for public office, lived in a neighboring district and said she had no intends to move. A House member only has to live in the state. Through October 14, Moore had spent $1,921,880 to Womack’s $55,626. He spent nearly $1 million on ads. She had no paid full-time staff and didn’t buy a TV spot. Three days after the deputy served her she was handing out T-shirts to striking workers at Charlotte Douglas airport. Moore won five of the six counties. He even won the Election Day vote by 21,246. But early in-person voting, which started four days after the deputy revealed up, gave Womack a 24,700 vote lead. With the felony case still pending, she posted, “#HatersGonnaHate I’m still Congresswoman-Elect.” On November 16 prosecutors learned she’d reached a deal with Budget. She paid the assessed rental cost for the overdue period. Budget told prosecutors it was satisfied. Campaign donations may not have mattered in the race, but that’s an unusually inexpensive way to buy goodwill with a member of the U.S. House of Representatives. On November 24 the state dismissed the charge with prejudice. This Wasn’t Hertz When I first wrote about Womack on October 11, my entire comment was “Ruh roh – it wasn’t Hertz.” A reader guessed Budget had lost track of a car it already had back. A father and his 13-year-old daughter were held at gunpoint outside Savannah in a car they’d just rented from Hertz’s Thrifty brand. When police let the father show them his rental agreement, it was 36 minutes old. The car had been reported stolen before Thrifty handed him the keys. A Hertz President’s Circle member wound up in jail over a Salt Lake City rental he’d extended, returned and paid $3,900 for. Those arrest stories seemed to dry up after Hertz brought in Palantir to help track its fleet in 2022 and agreed to pay $168 million to settle 364 claims. At Least Womack Was Still Campaigning North Carolina Republicans drew a map they expected would give them 11 of the state’s 14 U.S. House seats. Democrats won 11. Elsewhere the wave carried a couple of candidates who’d actually stopped campaigning. In Iowa, Eric Armstrong suspended his state House campaign on September 7 for health reasons. He beat a county supervisor and retired police lieutenant by about ten points. In Texas, Ericka Lomick suspended her campaign when a federal mortgage fraud conviction raised questions about whether she could serve. Her name stayed on the ballot for both the rest of the outgoing state representative’s term and the next one. She beat the same Republican in both elections. He’s asked the Texas Supreme Court to block certification of the special election. In California, Womack’s $55,626 would’ve looked like a fortune to Hipolito Cerros. The 28-year-old former mayor raised no campaign money, hired no staff and bought no ads. He unseated the Republican leader of the state Assembly. Tennessee tech support worker Victoria Broderick lost to Congressman Scott DesJarlais in 2024. He took 70% of the vote. After Republicans redrew the district, she ran again. She was still working full time and had to message her boss the morning after the election. The race was called for her the same day Womack’s charge was dropped. My personal favorite this cycle is Maricopa County, Arizona’s Sebastian Matta – a 19-year-old Arizona State philosophy sophomore – who beat a former state senator to become clerk of the Superior Court. He’d filed his campaign finance paperwork late and blamed his accountant for going quiet on him. He’ll run an office that processes 15,000 documents a day. To rent a Corolla from Budget at the Phoenix airport, he’s still two years short of the usual minimum age. In 2012, the anti-gay Democrat running as the incumbent for state representative in Hutchinson, Kanasa defeated her primary challenger – an openly gay son of a former member of the Ku Klux Klan – and then went on to best her Republican opponent who was a pro-gay rights, pro-choice train conductor named Dakota Bass. That race was featured in season two, episode eight of The Newsroom. (HT: Paul H.)     #111934. House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Rollcall ↗ Open Full Page

    House Democrats eye stock trading ban as early priority next Congress

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1327 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take.
    • After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.
    • But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the problem could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that house Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, here at a news conference on Capitol Hill last week, says banning stock trading in Congress is a “high priority.” Now Democrats must decide what form their push will take. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    After stock trading became a major talking point on the campaign trail this fall, Democrats are feeling pressure to push through a bill in the new year.

    But banning trading by members of Congress may not be easy, and some worry the problem could get bogged down in larger debates over the party’s anti-corruption agenda.

    “I’d rather have it be a clean bill focused on stock trading, and not muddy it by adding other topics, even if they’re good policies,” noted Rep. Seth Magaziner, D-R.I.

    Sources indicate that the incoming majority could plant a flag on government accountability with a broad package ranging from insider trading to campaign finance and more. Or they could zoom in on the stocks issue with a standalone bill.

    Magaziner said he hasn’t received any assurances from House Democratic leaders, instead describing a “collaborative conversation” about what form the legislation could take.

    “I worry that it would get weighed down under its own weight if you try to load it up with too many things,” Magaziner mentioned, while stressing he would support whatever expected incoming Speaker Hakeem Jeffries decides.

    Meanwhile, more than half of the Democrats in the incoming freshman class are calling for action on Day One of the latest Congress, sending a letter to Jeffries last week suggesting they make a “down payment on much-needed reform” by changing House rules to curb stock trading.

    In a recent development, “Democrats may have won the election, but we have a long way to go to earn back the trust of voters across the country,” reads the letter, led by Reps.-elect Sarah Trone Garriott of Iowa and Jamie Ager of North Carolina. “A stock trading ban alone will not fix Washington, but it is the fastest way to show voters we heard them.”.

    Folding new language into the House’s internal rules would be a relatively easy path, requiring just a majority vote on the House floor, instead of passage in both chambers and the president’s signature. But such internal limits wouldn’t have the force of law, and some believe it would cool the urgency around the problem while doing little to crack down on insider trading.

    Colorado Rep. Jason Crow said moving forward rapidly with a rule change wouldn’t preclude passing a bill, suggesting his fellow Democrats do both.

    Industry observers note that “I want to pursue a parallel track,” mentioned Crow, who co-chairs the End Corruption Caucus. “We want to move via rule and just prohibit it right out of the gate, or as much as we can.”.

    Jeffries has repeatedly said the topic is high on his to-do list as he looks to deliver on the accountability the “American people are demanding.”.

    In a recent development, “We’re committed to making sure we pass legislation that bans members of Congress from trading stocks. That will be a high priority,” he said at a news conference this week.

    But with more than two dozen different bills on the topic introduced over the past few years alone, lawmakers will have to decide exactly what a “ban” means to them.

    Recent findings suggest that some want to force members of Congress to fully offload their stocks with the exception of widely held mutual funds. Other proposals would block lawmakers from buying newly introduced stocks but allow them to keep the ones they already own, like a Republican-led bill that passed the House earlier this year but stalled in the Senate.

    Democrats resisted that push, which was led by outgoing House Administration Chair Bryan Steil, R-Wis., partly because it included an unrelated voter ID provision they called a “poison pill.” Many also complained the measure didn’t go far enough, extending to members’ spouses and dependent children but leaving out key figures in other branches of government, such as the president.

    Rep. Pramila Jayapal, D-Wash., said she wants to stay close to the text of a consensus bill she hammered out last year with a small bipartisan group that included Magaziner and Reps. Chip Roy, R-Texas, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Tim Burchett, R-Tenn., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa.

    “That is the most comprehensive, thorough, thoughtful proposal and bipartisan proposal that we have,” she said of the bill, dubbed the Restore Trust in Congress Act.

    That measure would not apply to President Donald Trump, as many Democrats have urged as they seek to draw attention to his ballooning wealth while in office. Still, Jayapal suggested a presidential stock trading ban could be moved separately.

    It has been revealed that “There is discussion about the president, vice president, Cabinet, Supreme Court. I know we’re working on some language around enforcement, around those pieces, but I actually think that can be a separate bill,” Jayapal noted. “We want to hold everyone accountable — but at minimum, we have to do ourselves.”.

    It’s not clear how much appetite will exist next year for a bipartisan compromise that could realistically clear a 60-vote cloture threshold in the Senate. Notably, key Republicans who worked on the consensus bill will be leaving Congress, with Roy losing a primary bid for Texas attorney general and Fitzpatrick unseated by a Democratic challenger.

    While lawmakers could in theory advance a new stock-trading bill even sooner, before Democrats take control of both chambers, time and patience is short in the lame-duck session.

    At a news conference at the Capitol earlier this week with Crow and Jayapal, a group of freshman and returning Democrats took matters into their own hands, promising not to hold or trade individual stocks as part of a broader pledge backed by the Political Integrity Project.

    In a recent development, “My district, Upcoming York 10, happens to include Wall Street, but I don’t represent Wall Street. I represent the people of Brooklyn and Manhattan who deserve someone who goes to work every single day and highlights right up front, ‘I work for you.’ And what better way to prove that than by day one showing we will ban members of Congress from enriching themselves, from trading stocks?” Rep.-elect Brad Lander noted.

    Sources indicate that while momentum has grown in recent years as key senior lawmakers softened their resistance to a stock trading bill, not everyone is on board. Some members still argue, whether publicly or privately, that they should be able to trade on the stock market just like other citizens or that existing disclosure requirements established by a 2012 law are already enough to discourage dubious trades.

    As they iron out the legislative text of any newly introduced bill, members will have to decide how to handle emerging topics such as prediction markets and crypto, along with sticky questions such as whether to allow blind trusts. And extending restrictions to the president could be a nonstarter for many Republicans.

    Industry observers note that sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., remarked Democrats in the next Congress should look to a bipartisan bill that advanced out of the Senate Homeland and Governmental Affairs Committee in July 2025 as a model.

    According to recent reports, “The legislation we passed out of the committee applied to the executive branch,” he said. “But it didn’t take effect for anybody until their next terms, which was a compromise.”.

    That proposal would apply to future presidents but not the current one, potentially freeing up more Republicans to vote for it without angering Trump. Still, it hasn’t seen action on the Senate floor.

    Hawley said that while he’d like to see a “full ban on trading and holding” in Congress, he would be open to a weaker proposal in the interest of getting something done.

    “I’ll take anything that’s an incremental improvement over what we have now, which is nothing,” he said.

    Aris Folley contributed to this report.

Federal Communications Commission (FCC) Chair Brendan Carr is a willing partner, going so far as to threaten the licenses of Disney-owned ABC stations with an early renewal proceeding. This highly unusual move (purportedly for unlawful discrimination) followed President Trump’s demand that ABC and NBC affiliates lose their broadcast licenses for unfavorable coverage of him.

    How did we get to a point where the president and FCC chair can threaten a broadcaster’s license over disfavored content? Two features of federal law enable this abuse: a vague public interest standard open to broad, subjective interpretation, and an archaic equal time rule.

    It has been revealed that brian A. Rankin is an adjunct fellow with the Competitive Enterprise Institute.

    At the Races: The upcoming Trump Democrats

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day.
    • By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.
    • Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that editor’s note: At the Races will not publish next week on Thanksgiving Day. We’ll be back the following week.

    By Niels Lesniewski, Mary Ellen McIntire and Daniela Altimari.

    Senate Democrats powered their way to a majority by flipping nine seats – their biggest gain in nearly 70 years.

    Eight of those wins were in states that Donald Trump has carried every time he’s run so it’s no surprise that some of the incoming senators are talking up the prospect of working with him over the next two years.

    Recent findings suggest that “We don't have time to wait until we have a different administration in the White House,” South Carolina Sen.-elect Annie Andrews told reporters this week. “We have two years ahead of us. We have very real problems that we need to address.”.

    According to recent reports, andrews is the first Democrat elected to the Senate from South Carolina since 1998. A pediatrician, she cited reducing prescription drug costs as a potential area of common ground with Trump.

    Recent findings suggest that “I support the president's attempts to stop taxes on tips and taxes on Social Security,” Andrews remarked, citing two selling points of last year’s GOP reconciliation law. During the campaign, she issued a policy paper expressing support for making those provisions of the tax code permanent.

    James Talarico, the incoming senator from Texas, told fellow Democrats gathered in Denver last week that if Trump wanted “the same plaques and portraits and busts as LBJ, we can help make that a reality.”.

    “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” stated Talarico, the first Democrat in nearly 40 years to win a Senate race in the Lone Star State.

    The idea of Trump and congressional Democrats working together might seem far-fetched, but with the incoming Democrats hailing from places such as Alaska, the Carolinas, Mississippi, Kansas and Texas, there’s a political incentive to appeal to Republican-leaning voters back home.

    But intentionally or not, Talarico and other newly elected Democrats might be borrowing from the playbook of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who has welcomed Trump when goals align, including on an effort to redevelop the Sunnyside rail yard in the president’s native Queens.

    Trump has stressed that he will veto legislation he opposes from the incoming Democratic Congress, but, at least for the moment, he seems open to deals.

    “I have a feeling that this is going to be an unbelievably productive two years,” Trump told Fox News early Thursday morning in Shenzhen, China, adding that  he would invite Democrats to the White House.

    In a recent development, “I respect them,” he stated. “Politics is a nasty game, and they won.”.

    Recent findings suggest that peltola prevails: Former Rep. Mary Peltola’s victory over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan in Alaska brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to 56 seats in the 120th Congress. Peltola finished with just over 50 percent of the vote, negating the need to use the state’s ranked choice voting system. The race for the state’s at-large House district was decided by a ranked choice tally, with Republican Rep. Nick Begich defeating independent Bill Hill 51 percent to 49 percent in the final round. Alaska voters also rejected an attempt to eliminate ranked choice voting in the state by a vote of 54 percent to 46 percent.

    Leadership elections: House Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next speaker in a 251-11 closed-door Wednesday vote, Roll Call’s Lauren Green reports. That puts Jeffries in prime position to become the first Black speaker when the full chamber votes in January. Meanwhile, Senate Democrats are scheduled to pick the next majority leader on Dec. 1, as our colleague Savannah Behrmann reports. Charles E. Schumer, who’s being challenged by Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen, maintains he has the votes to win.

    A victory lap and a warning: Even as the Congressional Hispanic Caucus celebrates its largest roster ever, the group’s leaders had a warning for their fellow Democrats: “Latino voters gave Democrats a two-year lease, but it expires in 2028 unless the party changes its playbook for good,” mentioned California Rep. Linda T. Sánchez, who leads the group’s campaign arm.

    #KYGOV: Republican Rep. James R. Comer, who was just elected to a sixth full term, released his much-anticipated run for Kentucky governor this week. The Bluegrass State is one of three states holding statewide executive  elections in 2027, along with Louisiana and Mississippi.

    Rocky Mountain roundup: Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken Republican with a national reputation as a Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for reelection in Colorado’s 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired Navy rear admiral. Meanwhile, Republican Gabe Evans, who fell short in his bid for a second term in the neighboring 8th District, announced he looks to challenge Laubacher in two years, Roll Call’s Samantha Freeman reports.

    In a recent development, they’re back: Our colleague Nina Heller tracked down former congressional staffers who are back on the Hill as newly elected members. “I never thought this would be the path, but I’m honored to do it,” noted Rep.-elect Sydney Gruters, who worked for fellow Florida Republicans Greg Steube and Vern Buchanan, her soon-to-be House predecessor.

    RIP: Former Rep. Jim McDermott, a longtime advocate for universal health care, died last week at the age of 89. The Washington Democrat, who retired to a small town in southwestern France after 28 years in the House, was hailed by his home state’s senior senator, Patty Murray, “as one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress.”.

    Where the House stands: As of 3 p.m. Eastern time, House Democrats have flipped 46 seats to three for the Republicans and are on track to hold at least 257 seats in the next Congress. Six races remain uncalled by The Associated Press, including two in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. The AP is also yet to call Tennessee’s 4th District, where Republican Rep. Scott DesJarlais has conceded to Democrat Victoria Broderick, who leads by 272 votes out of nearly 200,000 cast.

    According to recent reports, thompson loses: California Rep. Mike Thompson lost his bid for a 15th term to former venture capitalist Eric Jones, a political newcomer who poured millions into his campaign. Thompson is the second California member to lose to a fellow Democrat this year, after Rep. Jimmy Gomez. But Rep. Doris Matsui held off an intraparty challenge from democratic socialist Mai Vang.

    2028 draft: Supporters of former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg launched Team Pete PAC on Thursday, an effort to urge him to launch a second presidential bid.

    Battleground rep: Michigan Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet will be House Democrats' battleground leadership representative in the next Congress, acting as a bridge between members in competitive districts and party leadership. McDonald Rivet, who ran unopposed for the position, will succeed Nevada Rep. Susie Lee.

    Industry observers note that #INGOV: Indiana Gov. Mike Braun launched his 2028 reelection campaign as speculation swirls that state Attorney General Todd Rokita could challenge him for the Republican nomination. Rokita, a former congressman, has criticized Braun for not disciplining state educators who posted controversial comments after Charlie Kirk’s assassination but noted last week that he wanted Braun to “run for governor” and “be successful.” The two previously faced off in a 2018 Republican Senate primary, with Braun going on to serve one term in the Senate.

    Fresh leader for New Dems: Illinois Rep. Nikki Budzinski will chair the New Democrat Coalition next year, taking over from fellow Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider. New Mexico’s Gabe Vasquez, Ohio’s Greg Landsman and Washington’s Kim Schrier and Marilyn Strickland will serve as co-chairs of the center-left group, the largest ideological entity in the Democratic Caucus.

    Remembering Holden: Former Pennsylvania Rep. Tim Holden, who served 10 terms in the House before losing a Democratic primary to Matt Cartwright in 2012, died Sunday at the age of 69. House members held a moment of silence for Holden on the floor Thursday. Republican Rep. Dan Meuser, whose district includes territory Holden once represented, described him as “well-liked and widely respected, including by those on both sides of the political aisle.”.

    In a recent development, investigated: Ohio Rep.-elect Brian Poindexter is under investigation for alleged sexual harassment after the Democrat’s campaign hired a human resources firm to investigate the complaint. Both the Blue Dog PAC and the Congressional Progressive Caucus, which had endorsed Poindexter’s candidacy, dropped their support in the closing days of the campaign after learning of the allegation.

    Tennessee two-step: Tennessee Democrat Jeri Green, who narrowly lost the open governor’s race to Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, announced a bid for the state Senate seat GOP Rep.-elect Brent Taylor is expected to vacate. Taylor narrowly defeated Democratic state Rep. Justin Pearson in the redrawn 9th District, though both men were simultaneously reelected to their legislative seats.

    Industry observers note that the  historic “blue tsunami” that swept Democrats into commanding Senate and House majorities has some pundits questioning whether Republicans will ever be in charge again, observes Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections.

    But you just have to look at the election results from two years ago to realize that when it comes to winning party coalitions, nothing is permanent anymore, Nathan writes.

    Only the young: Latest York magazine catches up with young Republicans in South Carolina and finds that immigration policy and the war in Iran have turned many of the MAGA faithful against the GOP.

    From satirist to senator: The Washington Post traces South Carolina Democrat Annie Andrews’ journey from an online agitator who made relentless fun of Republicans to a newly elected senator who notes she’s eager to work with her GOP colleagues.

    Bad blood: The Boston Globe explores the long-standing rivalry between Maine’s two newest members of Congress: Democratic Sen.-elect Troy Jackson and Republican Rep.-elect Paul LePage.

    Schumer’s choice: Uncertainty around whether Schumer will seek another term in 2028 has risen as the Newly introduced York Democrat seeks to become Senate majority leader next year, Politico reports.

    That's how long it's been since the Senate Democratic Caucus last saw a contested race for its top leadership position, with Maryland’s Van Hollen now challenging Schumer for the job.

    Industry observers note that after Democrats lost eight Senate seats (and their majority) in the 1994 Republican Revolution, 42-year old South Dakota Sen. Tom Daschle edged out Connecticut's Christopher J. Dodd by a single vote, 24-23, to succeed outgoing leader George Mitchell of Maine.

    The last time a sitting Democratic Senate leader faced a formal challenge was a decade earlier, in 1984.

    Sources indicate that west Virginia's Robert C. Byrd, who’d been leading his party in the chamber since 1977, easily fended off a bid by Florida’s Lawton Chiles.

    It has been revealed that the last time either party experienced a contested race for the position was four years ago, when Florida Sen. Rick Scott challenged Republican leader Mitch McConnell of Kentucky.

    As Byrd did before him, McConnell handily defeated his challenger in the secret-ballot vote.

    Recent findings suggest that machine recounts in a pair of House races in North Carolina are expected to be completed Monday. Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx trails Democrat Chuck Hubbard by 331 votes, while GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan leads Democratic challenger Ashley Bell by just over 2,500 votes. The trailing candidate could then request a partial hand recount.

    In a recent development, monday is also the deadline for Republican Rep. Brad Finstad to formally request a recount in his razor-thin race against Democrat Jake Johnson in Minnesota’s 1st District. Finstad, who reportedly said he’ll seek one, trails Johnson by 321 votes.

    Gulf hotel owners have begun to reassess their hotel management agreements (HMAs) with operators, as the U.S.-Iran war that began in late February continues to weigh on the region’s hotels. So far, they are busy renegotiating terms rather than heading to arbitration.

    Under an HMA, an owner pays a brand to run the property, typically through a base fee tied to revenue that gets paid even when the hotel loses money. This leaves owners carrying most of the downside when performance falls short.

    Industry observers note that and many hotels in the Gulf have been underperforming for more than six months. Average daily rate dropped 28.1% to $181 and RevPAR fell 42% to $124.

    Dubai received 9.7 million international visitors in the first 10 months of 2026, down 38% from 15.7 million a year earlier, remarked Issam Kazim, CEO of the Dubai Corporation for Touri.

    House Ethics panel adopts changes aimed at speeding up investigations

    📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (661 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April.
    • In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.
    • In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ethics Chairman Michael Guest, left, and ranking member Mark DeSaulnier arrive for a committee meeting on Capitol Hill in April. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

    In a year roiled by sexual misconduct allegations in the House, the Ethics Committee approved a series of changes Thursday that its members say are intended to improve how the panel handles its investigations.

    In a rare public meeting lasting less than 10 minutes, the committee discussed proposed tweaks aimed at speeding up its processes, after some observers have criticized its pace.

    According to recent reports, “My problem with the Ethics Committee is it just takes too damn long,” Rep. Madeleine Dean, D-Pa., stated earlier this year.

    The internal rule changes were adopted in a voice vote by the committee, which is evenly divided between Republicans and Democrats.

    “We believe that these rule changes will provide more transparency. They will expedite our investigative process while maintaining protections for witnesses and victims, while also making sure that … due process is protected,” Chair Michael Guest, R-Miss., remarked during the meeting.

    Industry observers note that when former Reps. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., and Tony Gonzales, R-Texas, resigned earlier this year amid misconduct allegations, it sparked outrage as some called to rethink how the House polices bad behavior. Both men were on the radar of the Ethics Committee at the time, but such investigations have tended to move slowly.

    According to recent reports, “I want the Ethics Committee to move faster,” said panel member Rep. Suhas Subramanyam, D-Va., back in April.

    According to recent reports, the committee did not immediately make available the exact text of the changes it adopted Thursday. But a summary sent in a news release earlier this week included one proposal aimed at “consolidating deadlines” for a member to respond to an investigative subcommittee’s findings. Another tweak aimed at speeding things up would give the chair and ranking member subpoena power on behalf of the committee, rather than requiring a full committee vote.

    The summary described “codifying the Committee’s policy of publicly disclosing any findings that a Member engaged in sexual harassment or other sexual misconduct” while “prohibiting publication of the identity of any victim.”.

    Also on the list: “Expanding the circumstances under which fines and denials of privileges are considered an appropriate sanction to include any abuses of position.”.

    It comes as women on both sides of the aisle have formed a partnership aimed at reviewing how Congress deals with sexual misconduct and suggesting concrete ideas for an overhaul. Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., has been co-leading that effort as the chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus alongside Republican Women’s Caucus head Kat Cammack, R-Fla.

    According to Leger Fernández, the Ethics Committee has “consulted” with her group as it weighed the changes to its internal rules.

    “The Ethics Committee was clearly listening to women staffers, and has been a great partner in our work. We appreciate how they’ve consulted DWC and that these proposals will improve transparency and help protect the identities of those who report alleged misconduct. Together with RWC, we will continue to work on additional legislation in our sexual misconduct reform agenda,” she remarked in a statement earlier this week.

    Cammack stated that, while “the entire system on Capitol Hill has been designed to create a chilling effect for victims,” the Ethics committee rule changes would help.

    Sources indicate that “Putting public disclosure of misconduct findings in writing, while protecting every victim’s identity, gives staffers a commitment they can count on. Faster investigations mean they get answers in time to matter,” Cammack mentioned in a statement. “This is exactly the kind of change our bipartisan task force has been pushing for.”.

    AirAsia’s Q3 Reveals Why Fernandes Pushed the Comeback to 2028

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that photo Credit: An AirAsia A320 neo jet, manufactured by Airbus.
    • According to recent reports, airAsia has shown it can charge more.
    • AirAsia Group posted a smaller third-quarter loss on Monday as higher fares made up for most of the jump in fuel costs, but the results show why Tony Fernandes pushed the comeback to 2028: a smaller AirAsia costs more to run, and it is still losing money.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that photo Credit: An AirAsia A320 neo jet, manufactured by Airbus. AirAsia Group.

    According to recent reports, airAsia has shown it can charge more. It hasn't shown it can make money at its new, smaller size. Until the $1 billion debt financing lands, the balance sheet, not demand, decides when the comeback starts.

    AirAsia Group posted a smaller third-quarter loss on Monday as higher fares made up for most of the jump in fuel costs, but the results show why Tony Fernandes pushed the comeback to 2028: a smaller AirAsia costs more to run, and it is still losing money.

    Industry observers note that airAsia Group, the listed tech giant that now houses all of AirAsia’s airlines, posted a loss attributable to shareholders of RM175 million ($43 million), according to its third-quarter results. That’s about a third of its second-quarter loss. Most of the improvement came from charging more, helped by jet fuel easing from its second-quarter peak. Planes stayed nearly as full as fares rose sharply, and that won back much of what the jet fuel spike had taken earlier in the year.

    Including minority interests, the loss after tax was RM381.3 million ($93 million). Revenue fell 11% from a year earlier to RM4.66 billion, and 8% from the second quarter.

    “Our third quarter performance suggests that the worst is behind us,” CEO Bo Lingam said in a statement. AirAsia is a smaller airline than it was a year ago, and a smaller low-cost airline is an expensive one to run. It still spends more to fly each seat than it earns from it, and its equity cushion is thin, with shareholders’ equity of RM362 million. The refinancing it needs to steady the balance sheet, which AirAsia targeted for this quarter and as recently as last week expected by December or January, is now due to conclude in the fourth quarter or early 2027.

    According to recent reports, the results came the same day Thai Airways reported its own third-quarter loss on fuel costs. If jet fuel eases as AirAsia expects in 2027, higher fares could start turning into profit across the region. For AirAsia, the question is whether that comes fast enough.

    AirAsia consolidated its Malaysian, Thai, Indonesian, Philippine and Cambodian airlines with AirAsia X in January. This was the first quarter in which the merged group had almost no seats left that were sold before the fuel shock, which let it reprice. Average fares rose by almost a quarter from a year earlier, while the share of filled seats barely moved.

    The group suspended 76 routes in the third quarter, mostly fuel-heavy international flights to India, China and Australia, and kept most of its flying close to home, where demand held up best. The retreat has cost it ground. Malaysia Airlines this month overtook the AirAsia group as the largest operator between Malaysia and India for the first time since 2021, though Fernandes has dismissed suggestions that rivals could take the lead for internal Malaysia flights.

    According to recent reports, airAsia cut what it spends on staff, airport charges and leases, but its remaining fixed costs were spread over far fewer seats, so the cost of flying each one rose. Higher fares more than covered the extra fuel bill. The rise in other costs per passenger then took back part of that gain.

    Sources indicate that not every market pulled its weight. Malaysia and Cambodia were profitable at the operating level, Indonesia and the Philippines lost less than a year earlier, and Thailand had a weak quarter. Currency losses added to the damage further down the income statement.

    It has been revealed that fuel is squeezing AirAsia’s regional rivals too. Cebu Pacific’s management noted this month it has pretty much no chance of making money this year, and Thai Airways’ finance chief warned that if current oil prices become the upcoming normal then its third-quarter loss could be a guide to performance in the fourth.

    Industry observers note that airAsia is handing back older, more expensive aircraft: 25 of them this year and most of them early. And it says it may return more in 2027. That move cuts lease bills but leaves less room to grow, six months after the group placed a record order for 150 Airbus A220s. Many of the planes it keeps aren’t flying either. About 31% of the 234 aircraft in the group’s main fleet were out of service at the end of September, mostly for scheduled maintenance, with engine problems among the other causes.

    That trade-off worries some analysts. Handing back jets now could slow AirAsia’s eventual comeback, analysts told Skift this month, because fresh narrowbody delivery slots are scarce until around 2033.

    The pressure point is funding. AirAsia ended June with far less cash than it owed within the year. It is working on up to $1 billion in debt financing and states talks with creditors are progressing.

    The strain has been visible for months. In September, Endau Analytics’ Shukor Yusof questioned the airline’s financial resilience, citing its balance sheet and reports of delayed rental payments. Fernandes insisted that no aircraft had been grounded over nonpayment, and he has denied reports of a government-backed contingency plan. Malaysia’s transport and finance ministries remain in talks with the airline.

    Industry observers note that for now, management is betting on the year-end peak. It plans to add back capacity in the fourth quarter, restore some routes and keep pushing fares higher — and states forward bookings are running in line with last year, at elevated yields. The Q3 presentation called 2026 and 2027 a “reset” and 2028 the “rebuild,” when fresh fuel-efficient jets begin arriving. It gave no passenger targets for 2027.

    Fernandes has been somewhat blunter. In a LinkedIn post last week, he called 2027 “a period of consolidation” and warned of “more painful decisions” on costs, without repeating his September target of 80 million passengers next year. Expansion elsewhere is on hold too: the group’s Bahrain hub is now targeted for March 2027, should conditions in the Gulf allow.

    • Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., seen here at the Capitol on June 17, noted additional war powers votes are under discussion for when Democrats control both chambers in the 120th Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

    It has been revealed that the Senate rejected a resolution Thursday meant to rebuke President Donald Trump over the Iran war weeks after the midterm elections demonstrated the depth of public anger about the war and its effects on the U.S. economy.

    Senators voted 48-51 against adopting the Iran war powers resolution that the House previously adopted in mid-September that would direct the president to withdraw U.S. forces from the war.

    As they have previously with similar measures, GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky broke with their party to support the resolution, while Democratic Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania broke with his party to oppose it. Departing GOP Sens. Thom Tillis of North Carolina and Bill Cassidy of Louisiana, who have at times voted in support of similar measures, this time voted against the resolution.

    Even if the resolution was adopted in both chambers of Congress, it would be largely symbolic since, as a concurrent resolution, it would not go to the president for his signature.

    But the vote afforded senators the opportunity to register their complaints about the war for the first time since Democrats routed Republicans in the midterm elections.

    It also comes amid a larger debate within the Democratic Party on how best to fulfill their campaign promise of ending the war as they prepare to take control of Congress next year.

    Democrats have become increasingly interested in trying to cut off funding for the war rather than continuing to hold war powers votes. But they are divided on whether to demand an immediate end to funding in the next government funding bill in December or to wait until they take power in January.

    “When we have the gavels, we are contemplating other things, and we're actually contemplating things in connection with the CR discussion,” Sen. Tim Kaine, D-Va., told reporters Thursday in an apparent reference to the debate among Democrats.

    According to recent reports, as of Nov. 13, the war has cost at least $48.3 billion, up from $47 billion last month, the nominee to be Navy comptroller, Arthur Miller, told the Senate Armed Services Committee at his confirmation hearing Thursday.

    According to recent reports, as with previous estimates, the number Miller cited Thursday includes munitions, equipment replacement costs and operational costs but does not factor in the cost of damage to U.S. bases, which alone is likely to run in the billions.

    It has been revealed that last week, a trio of Senate Democrats unveiled legislation to prohibit funding for offensive military operations in Iran that they said they intend to introduce as an amendment to the next government funding bill, which Congress will need to pass to avoid a government shutdown after Dec. 11.

    On Thursday as the Senate voted on the war powers resolution, Sens. Tammy Duckworth, D-Ill., and Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., two of the sponsors of the proposed amendment, demanded it be included in the next funding bill.

    “We’ve already tried tool after tool to get the president to rein in this conflict. Nine months in, defunding the war is the only way to force Trump to end it,” Duckworth, who vowed to vote against any continuing resolution that doesn’t include the amendment, said at a news conference.

    Recent findings suggest that sen. Michael Bennet, D-Colo., unveiled his own proposed amendment Thursday to bar any future and previous funding from being used to “support directly or indirectly combat activities by United States personnel in or over Iran, or in Iranian territorial waters” unless specifically authorized by Congress.

    His legislation is modeled off of language Congress passed in 1973 to cut off funding for the Nixon administration’s bombing campaign in Cambodia, Bennet’s office noted in a news release.

    “When we vote on short-term spending in the near future, we can fund the government and end this war. It is what the American people demand, and what they deserve,” Bennet said in a statement.

    Meanwhile, the House is likely to vote again on a war powers resolution before year’s end.

    According to recent reports, “Before the lame duck’s over, I hope to enforce a war powers resolution vote, and it’ll be a chance for Republicans to say whether they did or didn’t get the message on Nov. 3,” Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., mentioned Thursday in a brief interview, referring to the date of the elections.

    According to recent reports, as with previous resolutions, Massie’s would direct the president to remove U.S. military units from hostilities against Iran unless specifically authorized by Congress or needed to defend against an imminent attack.

    In a recent development, the resolution was filed Nov. 10, and under the 1973 War Powers Resolution, Massie can force a vote 15 calendar days after its introduction.

    John M. Donnelly and Lauren Green contributed to this report.

    #111920. Tech Report: Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (556 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nationalreview ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Hakeem Jeffries’s Reckless Medicare Expansion

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (556 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nationalreview

    ⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that we have long warned that if Republicans did not get serious about advancing their own vision for health care, Democrats would use their next opportunity to further expand the role of government.
    • According to recent reports, fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made a radical proposal.
    • No doubt, with a stampede of newly introduced socialists joining his caucus, Jeffries is trying to get ahead of the left-wing push for a fully government-run system branded as “Medicare for All.” When last nationally debated in 2019, it was estimated to add $34 trillion to existing federal spending with no plausible financing mechanism.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that we have long warned that if Republicans did not get serious about advancing their own vision for health care, Democrats would use their next opportunity to further expand the role of government. And here we are.

    According to recent reports, fresh off a sweeping victory in the midterm elections, incoming House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries made a radical proposal. He endorsed lowering the retirement age of Medicare and adding vision, hearing, and dental coverage to the program. Additionally, he said that the government should provide coverage for all children.

    No doubt, with a stampede of newly introduced socialists joining his caucus, Jeffries is trying to get ahead of the left-wing push for a fully government-run system branded as “Medicare for All.” When last nationally debated in 2019, it was estimated to add $34 trillion to existing federal spending with no plausible financing mechanism.

    Industry observers note that at this point, Jeffries’s proposal is theoretical. There’s a significant budgetary difference between lowering the Medicare eligibility age from its current 65 to 60, and lowering it to 50 — as Senator Kirsten Gillibrand and other senators are proposing. There are also questions about what sort of premiums, if any, would be required for near-retirees to “buy in” to the program or how generous the theoretical vision, hearing, and dental benefits would be. Filling in those blanks is the difference between a proposal that costs a few hundred billion dollars and one that costs trillions of dollars.

    According to recent reports, but it’s preposterous at this stage to start any discussion of Medicare with a suggestion that spending on the program needs to be increased rather than reined in — especially to cover a population without a high uninsured rate. Over the next decade, the federal government is projected to spend $18.5 trillion on Medicare, making it the largest expenditure apart from that other federal entitlement, Social Security. Medicare no longer collects enough money in payroll taxes to cover current benefits, let alone added benefits that cover more people. Even a more modest lowering of the retirement age to 60 would add over 7 million beneficiaries. On its current trajectory, Medicare’s trust fund (the money it is “owed” by the rest of the government from the days when it was running surpluses) would be exhausted by 2033.

    Medicare is a major driver of the nation’s broader fiscal problem. Already, debt held by the public has eclipsed 100 percent of gross domestic product. By the end of the decade, it is projected to reach 120 percent. By comparison, debt peaked at 106 percent during World War II. Now we are on track to exceed that number, not during a global crisis, but during an ordinary period of relative peace and prosperity. And that’s before Jeffries grabs the gavel with a massive majority behind him.

    Perhaps more concerning, President Trump indicated last week that he may be game for some compromise proposal. “There is a real possibility that we get a lot of great things done, especially on health care,” he said.

    If Trump is serious and actually considers cutting a deal with Democrats to expand Medicare, congressional Republicans should fight it at all costs.

    The Editors comprise the senior editorial staff of National Review magazine and nationalreview.com.

  • Both cards share core benefits such as priority boarding and credits for expedited airport security programs, but differ in the level and frequency of travel-related perks.
  • Upgrading may be worthwhile for those who regularly check multiple bags, use airline credits or pursue elite status, while occasional travelers may find the lower-tier card sufficient.
  • To receive checked bag benefits, your loyalty program number must be included in the reservation and tickets must be purchased with the eligible card.
  • Statement credits for services like ride-hailing and grocery delivery require activation and may have specific expiration dates or booking requirements.
  • Upgrading does not typically provide a new cardholder bonus, so applying for a new account may be preferable if eligible.
